to quantify a portion of the Bank's Scope 3 emissions, speciﬁcally the "Employee Commuting" category. 
Although these results do not represent the full Scope 3 emissions, they provide an initial estimate that will 
inform our future action plans and reporting. 
We employed a distance-based approach to calculate the employee commuting emissions, ensuring an 
accurate estimation based on the data formats provided by the third party. The recommended GHG Protocol 
approach was utilized, integrating the most updated and appropriate emission factors to evaluate the total 
emissions for the employee commuting category. 
These ﬁndings mark a signiﬁcant step in our commitment to sustainability. Future reports will expand on 
these initial results, incorporating additional Scope 3 categories and offering deeper insights into our ongoing 
sustainability initiatives. This approach underscores our dedication to understanding and mitigating our 
environmental impact, guiding us toward more effective and comprehensive sustainability and carbon emis-
sions reduction strategies.

External: Local 
The local benchmarking methodology was established by comparing emissions intensities (per m 2 and per 
FTE) with data published and reported from other ﬁnancial business peers. For this year’s report, the compari-
son focused solely on Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions intensities to ensure fairness and accuracy in the insights 
obtained. This approach helps to understand AAIB's performance and its position relative to its peers.
Data from eight different local ﬁnancial business peers, who published their carbon footprint studies between 
2021 and 2023, were collected. To maintain conﬁdentiality and avoid conﬂicts, the peers' names were 
anonymized and labeled from A to H. This anonymization allows for meaningful tracking of benchmarking 
results while preserving privacy.

External: Climate Impact Scoring (CIS)
The Climate Impact Scoring (CIS) system developed by ESG& employs a robust methodology designed to 
assess and quantify the climate performance of Egyptian banks. The methodology encompasses several key 
components to ensure comprehensive evaluation across national, MENA, and global standards:
1. Criteria Selection: The CIS system selects criteria that are most relevant and impactful for evaluating climate 
initiatives in the ﬁnancial sector. This includes but is not limited to carbon emissions accounting, ﬁnanced 
emissions, emissions reporting, decarbonization plans, carbon reduction actions, and sustainable ﬁnancial 
schemes.
2. Quantitative Assessment: Each criterion within the CIS system is quantitatively evaluated based on 
predeﬁned metrics and benchmarks. This ensures objective measurement of banks' performance in manag-
ing and reducing their carbon footprint, promoting transparency and comparability.
3. Scoring Framework: A structured scoring framework is applied to assign scores to banks based on their 
performance against the deﬁned criteria. Scores provide a clear indication of climate performance, ranging

4. Data Collection and Veriﬁcation: Rigorous data collection processes are employed to gather accurate and 
reliable information on banks' climate-related activities and impacts. Veriﬁcation mechanisms ensure the 
integrity and credibility of reported data.
5. Integration of International Standards: The CIS system integrates international standards and frameworks 
such as the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) to align assessment practices with 
global best practices in climate governance and reporting.
6. Continuous Improvement: The CIS methodology undergoes continuous reﬁnement and adaptation to 
reﬂect evolving climate science, regulatory requirements, and industry best practices. This ensures that the 
assessment remains relevant and effective in driving meaningful climate action among Egyptian ﬁnancial 
institutions.
By employing this methodology, the CIS system provides a comprehensive and systematic approach to evalu-
ating and promoting climate resilience and sustainability within the Egyptian ﬁnancial sector. It equips banks 
with actionable insights to enhance their climate strategies and contribute to global efforts in mitigating 
climate change impacts.

Data Quality Matrix
The Data Quality Matrix developed by ESG& integrates the reporting principles of the GHG Protocol to quantify 
and score the GHG data quality and materiality of banking sector institutions during carbon footprint report-
ing. The Matrix is grounded in the ﬁve principles of the GHG Protocol: Accuracy, Completeness, Transparency, 
Consistency, and Relevance. 
Accuracy ensures that data is free from signiﬁcant errors or biases, collected with precise methods, and 
validated through robust quality control measures.  
Completeness involves the inclusion of all relevant emissions sources, ensuring a comprehensive assessment.

2. Identiﬁed all projects and activities that took place during reporting periods.
3. Prepared customized data collection sheet and collected relevant data from departments.
4. Deﬁned all assumptions and exclusions.
5. Calculated GHG emissions under Scope 1 & 2;
6. Assessed the data quality and identiﬁed hotspots; and Provided recommendations to improve the data

Opening Remarks
About this Report
The Arab African International Bank (AAIB) is delighted 
to publish its Sustainability Report for the 2023 fiscal 
year. This report demonstrates our compliance with 
Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting 
standards, highlighting our performance and initiatives. 
It also reflects our dedication to transparency with all our 
stakeholders. Looking ahead, as we continue to strengthen 
and advance our commitment to sustainability, we are 
committed to consistently sharing our progress and 
accomplishments with stakeholders every year. 
In this report, we detail AAIB’s ESG performance, with 
a focus on the Bank’s identified material issues. All 
data included relate solely to Arab African International 
Bank as a standalone entity, including all operations in 
Egypt, UAE, and Lebanon, unless otherwise specified. For 
financial figures, the average foreign currency exchange 
rate applied is 30.6528 EGP per USD, while the closing rate 
used is 30.8144 EGP per USD.
The report covers the period from January 1, 2023, to 
December 31, 2023. Disclosures made after these dates are 
included only if relevant to the report’s context.
AAIB has reported in accordance with the 2021 GRI 
Standards. Additionally, the report outlines alignment 
with the UN Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs), 
as well as the SASB Standards on Commercial Banks and 
Consumer Finance, the TCFD Recommendations, and the 
UN Global Compact (UNGC) Principles.

Dear Stakeholders,
I am pleased to share with you the Arab African International 
Bank (AAIB)’s Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) 
Report, which highlights our progress and achievements in 
sustainability for the fiscal year 2023.
AAIB: A Legacy of Sustainable Banking
AAIB has been a pioneer in responsible banking in Egypt 
for over two decades. Since embracing an integrated ESG 
approach in 2003 and becoming Egypt’s first Bank to 
adopt the UN Global Compact principles in 2005, we have 
consistently championed sustainability. Our 2021-2025 strategy 
further embeds this commitment by prioritizing strategic 
agility, strong customer-centricity, and resilience amidst 
changing market dynamics, all while keeping environmental 
responsibility at the core of our operations.
Reflecting on 2023: A Year of Growth and Impact
In 2023, AAIB achieved outstanding financial results, 
demonstrating our resilience and strategic foresight in a 
dynamic economic environment. We achieved unprecedented 
real growth in total deposits, reaching 64% year-over-year, 
an impressive 80% growth compared to our peers. This 
momentum, culminating in a total deposit base of USD 12.7 
billion, provides us with a firm foundation for future growth. 
Additionally, we delivered a net profit of USD 228 million, a 
72% real growth. These robust financial results empower us 
to further invest in sustainable initiatives, responsible lending

Sustainable Finance: Investing in a Better Future
AAIB is unwavering in its commitment to sustainable finance. 
It recognizes that responsible banking is not just a good 
practice but a catalyst for positive change, ensuring that 
our activities benefit both our stakeholders and the planet. 
In 2023, our total lending for high-impact environmental 
and social projects surpassed USD 121 million. This portfolio 
actively drives progress across key areas, with USD 106 million 
financing vital environmental projects, including renewable 
energy and water efficiency initiatives, and USD 15 million 
dedicated to social projects spanning healthcare, education, 
and vital infrastructure. These strategic investments are 
building a more resilient and equitable Egypt, demonstrating 
the power of finance to create a brighter future for all.

About the Bank
Founded in 1964, the Arab African International Bank (AAIB) 
holds the distinction of being Egypt’s inaugural multinational 
bank, established by Special Law as a Joint Venture between 
the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) at 49.37% and the Kuwait 
Investment Authority (KIA) also at 49.37%. AAIB has grown 
into a premier regional banking institution, offering a 
comprehensive range of innovative products and services 
that include retail and corporate banking, SMEs, transaction 
banking solutions, investment banking, brokerage services 
through Arab African International Securities (AAIS), asset 
management through Arab African Investment Management 
(AAIM), private equity, leasing through Arab African 
International Leasing Company (AAIL), mortgage financing 
through Arab African International Mortgage Finance (AAIMF), 
and micro-enterprise solutions through Sandah.
Driven by the goal to serve as the gateway for international 
business into the region, the Bank is determined to enhance 
the potential and growth of its stakeholders across various 
segments, industries, sectors, geographies, and business 
cycles. As a leading financial institution, AAIB leverages its 
extensive expertise and capacities to achieve exceptional 
outcomes while upholding responsible banking and 
promoting sustainable growth.

record in sustainability and developed a clear, forward-thinking vision for growth. At AAIB, we believe that leadership in a 
major financial group goes beyond financial metrics—it requires a commitment to societal and environmental responsibilities 
through sustainable finance, all while staying true to our core values. 
AAIB was the first in the MENA region to integrate sustainable finance fully into the banking industry, setting a precedent and 
shaping industry trends. Our active participation in prominent international networks further distinguishes our sustainability 
efforts, demonstrating our ongoing dedication to sustainability leadership.
As we grow, we continue to align our growth with a strong sustainability framework. AAIB aims for a sustainable future built 
on foundational pillars that integrate environmental responsibility, social equity, and economic prosperity into our financial 
services. These pillars guide our actions and aspirations as we lead the way in building a sustainable economy, resilient 
communities, and a healthier environment.

Assessing Our Impact
In 2023, AAIB conducted its first materiality assessment 
to identify and prioritize critical issues pertinent to its 
operations and national context. This process followed a 
four-step approach:
AAIB began by examining its strategic priorities in 
conjunction with Egypt’s national strategies and goals. 
This step involved assessing industry trends and the 
regulatory framework set by the Central Bank of Egypt 
(CBE), ensuring alignment with Egypt’s Vision 2030 
objectives.
Following the contextual analysis, AAIB compiled an 
extensive list of industry-specific topics, guided by global 
standards such as GRI and SASB, as well as insights from 
ESG rating platforms. This list was then refined to focus 
on topics most relevant to the national context and 
AAIB’s strategic goals.
To gain a well-rounded view, AAIB consulted with 
stakeholders through surveys, workshops, and interviews 
with internal stakeholders, including employees, 
department heads, and executives, to gather valuable 
insights into the significance of various topics.
Using stakeholder feedback, AAIB evaluated and 
prioritized the identified material topics. This process 
included assessing alignment with national priorities, 
CBE regulations, and AAIB’s operational framework. Each 
topic was validated and ranked based on its importance

Corporate Governance Framework
At AAIB, we believe that strong governance is fundamental to sustainable growth. 
Every team member shares our resolve to create enduring value, which a corporate 
governance framework upholds. This framework is the cornerstone of AAIB’s 
success story, guiding how we conduct business and cultivate relationships with 
our stakeholders.
Designed to safeguard the interests of all stakeholders, ensure compliance with 
regulatory standards, and optimize organizational efficiency, AAIB’s governance 
framework encompasses a well-defined organizational structure that delineates 
roles and responsibilities clearly. Moreover, it outlines distinct mandates for the 
Board of Directors (BoD) and its sub-committees, as well as for management 
and management committees governing the operations of the Bank. AAIB has 
established a set of guidelines overseen by the BoD, while a dedicated Corporate 
Governance Committee is responsible for implementing and updating these 
guidelines as necessary.

Responsibilities of the Board of Directors 
The AAIB Board of Directors sets the Bank’s strategic 
direction and oversees its business and management 
performance. It ensures all activities align with shareholder 
interests and comply with governing laws, regulations, and 
internal policies.
In terms of management and oversight, the Board is 
responsible for approving corporate policies, especially 
those related to risk management, information technology 
and security, remuneration, and new product programs. 
It ensures AAIB has effective internal control and risk 
management systems supported by appropriate structures, 
policies, and procedures. It also approves the main 
organizational structure, facilitating effective decision-
making with clear lines of responsibility and accountability. 
Non-executive directors are required to meet with the 
Chairman independently of executive directors at least once 
a year.
Regarding strategic business planning, the Board approves 
the Bank’s strategy and business plans, which must align 
with its accepted risk appetite, and regularly reviews the 
implementation of these plans. The Board also approves the 
opening of branches or offices abroad. When it comes to 
decisions affecting the Bank’s shareholder equity, the Board 
is responsible for actions such as forming extraordinary 
reserves or reallocating reserves for purposes other than 
initially approved.
Other responsibilities include appointing the Chairman

Audit Committee
The Board Audit Committee (BAC) at AAIB primarily assists the Board in overseeing the quality and integrity of the Bank’s financial statements, ensuring compliance with legal 
and regulatory requirements, and assessing the qualifications, independence, and performance of both external auditors and the internal audit function. This role is defined by 
the Central Bank of Egypt, Banking Sector, and Money Law No. 194 of 2020, along with the Executive Regulations of Law No. 88 of 2003 and CBE Circular 95 on the Governance 
of Banks.
The BAC’s authorities and responsibilities include proposing the appointment and remuneration of external auditors, evaluating their independence, and reviewing any additional 
services they may provide. The committee discusses relevant issues with the Group’s Chief Audit Executive, Head of Compliance, and executive officers and studies the annual 
financial statements before submitting them to the Board. The BAC ensures the financial statements align with CBE rules and facilitates coordination between internal and 
external audits.
The committee reviews and approves the annual internal audit plan, assesses internal audit reports on the adequacy of control systems, and monitors compliance with 
recommendations. It also evaluates reports from the Head of Compliance regarding legislative and regulatory adherence and addresses any obstacles to internal auditing and

Risk Committee
The Board Risk Committee (BRC) at AAIB assists the Board in overseeing the Bank’s risk management and control framework, ensuring the adequacy and compliance of risk and 
control policies. The BRC is responsible for recommending the Board’s approval of risk management strategies and policies, including those related to capital management, liquidity, 
credit, market, operational risks, compliance, and reputation. They also endorse the appointment, performance, and removal of the Head of Risk, review the risk management 
division’s structure, and assess the Bank’s overall risk appetite.
The BRC evaluates macroeconomic and financial environments, regulatory changes, and strategic acquisitions or disposals, ensuring due diligence and risk assessments are 
conducted. They review risk capital charges, the effectiveness of the Bank’s risk management framework, and internal control systems. This involves monitoring large exposures,

They also advise the Remuneration Committee on aligning remuneration with risk appetite, reviewing major risk-related findings and management responses, and ensuring

review and update the Bank’s Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, evaluate reports for transparency, and endorse the annual governance report. The CGC inducts new Board

party transactions, assess changes in Board members’ status or affiliations, and regularly evaluate the performance of the Board and its committees. The CGC also reviews and 
updates the charters of Board committees and handles additional responsibilities as delegated by the Board.

Remuneration Committee
The Remuneration Committee (RemCo) at AAIB oversees the Bank’s compensation and incentive structures to ensure they align with performance, corporate governance standards, 
and applicable laws. RemCo determines and approves the CEO’s compensation, including salary, incentives, and benefits, and reviews the incentive packages for executive officers. 
The committee evaluates the CEO’s performance against the Bank’s goals and makes recommendations on their remuneration.
RemCo also reviews and recommends compensation for the Board’s Chair and non-executive members, considering peer institution practices. It ensures coherent bank-wide 
remuneration policies that fairly reward executives and reviews new benefit and equity plans for senior executives. The committee approves remuneration for control functions to 
maintain independence, reviews the annual bonus pool based on performance indicators, and assesses market remuneration trends. Additionally, RemCo approves remuneration 
arrangements outside the Bank’s policy and adapts policies to changing conditions, carrying out any additional responsibilities delegated by the Board.

staff members. The Code is designed to integrate ethical conduct into AAIB’s business practices. While not replacing 
existing manuals or policies, it comprehensively addresses various ethical and legal challenges that staff encounter daily. 
It guides their decision-making by fostering an understanding of the ethical implications and boundaries associated 
with their actions.
The Code is disseminated to all staff members, and new hires receive orientation as part of their foundational training. The 
HR Division ensures compliance with the Code of Conduct in collaboration with other relevant departments. Furthermore, 
the Corporate Governance Committee periodically reviews the Code to ensure its relevance and effectiveness.

monetary gifts, regardless of the amount, with violations potentially leading to disciplinary action. While we encourage positive

During the reporting period, the Compliance Function

At AAIB, we recognize that addressing corruption requires a 
dual approach of prevention and response. While regulatory 
compliance is key, we believe prevention requires cultivating 
the right culture. Through ongoing training, employees 
understand not just policies but also how even small acts 
of misconduct can severely undermine their work, career 
prospects, and the Bank’s relationships.
We believe that good governance must evolve with 
changing dynamics. By closely monitoring developments, 
we regularly review our programs and controls to 
promptly address new challenges through best practice 
implementation. This dual focus on shaping mindsets and

AAIB’s Whistleblowing policy and procedures enable 
employees to report alleged malpractice internally, 
ensuring management can investigate and take 
appropriate action. The policy provides a confidential 
channel for staff to raise concerns without fear of 
retaliation and applies to all representatives of AAIB. 
Employees making disclosures must reasonably believe 
that a criminal offense has been, is being, or is likely 
to be committed; that someone has failed, is failing, or 
is likely to fail to comply with any legal or regulatory 
obligation; or that the work environment has been, is 
being, or is likely to be damaged. Other concerns include 
breaches of Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Know Your 
Customer (KYC), Sanctions Policy & Procedures, and 
CBE regulations; information regarding a colleague’s 
involvement in illegal acts sourced from the media; 
employees inquiring about a customer without a valid 
reason or regulatory/control function requirement; and 
any action leading to actual or potential losses.

AAIB adopts the Equator Principles (EPs), a globally recognized set of guidelines for managing environmental and social 
risks in project financing, making it the first Egyptian institution to adopt these principles. The Bank expanded its risk 
management framework to include environmental and social (E&S) risks alongside traditional credit, market, operational, 
and liquidity risks. This expansion is crucial as it addresses the indirect contributions of banks to GHG emissions through 
their financing and lending activities.
AAIB’s internal policies, procedures, and active staff engagement support the framework provided by the EPs for 
identifying and managing E&S risks in project-related transactions. The Bank has further solidified its resolve to 
implement an E&S Policy that aligns with the IFC’s performance standards and the EPs. This policy integrates E&S 
risks into the Bank’s overall credit risk assessment framework, guiding transaction reviews, client advisory services, and 
promoting responsible business practices. To tackle E&S risks, including biodiversity-related risks, AAIB has engaged 
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) consultants to conduct assessments addressing environmental risks and 
hazards associated with prospective financing projects.

Environmental and Social Risk Management in Lending
E&S Policy: A Framework for Sustainable Lending
The AAIB Environmental and Social (E&S) Policy, first initiated and approved in March 2019, was updated and 
approved in March 2024. Beginning in 2024, AAIB will fully establish and implement this comprehensive policy 
framework, which applies to all financial lending activities across the Bank, including its international branches and 
subsidiaries where AAIB holds majority ownership. The E&S Policy outlines a rigorous screening process and risk 
assessment framework developed in line with the EBRD and IFC performance standards, as well as the Equator 
Principles. It details the integration of environmental and social considerations into credit decision-making, ensuring 
full compliance with national legislation in Egypt and the UAE. The policy sets clear environmental and social 
performance requirements for borrowers, defining roles and responsibilities for both AAIB and its borrowers to 
achieve sustainable outcomes. Additionally, the policy promotes strategic goals to support borrowers with high 
environmental and social benefits.

held at Sandah’s headquarters – the Bank’s microfinance arm, marking the initial phase of the Bank’s ESMS workflow

AAIB is prioritizing the integration of climate risks 
and opportunities within its credit risk assessment 
framework as part of its commitment to sustainable 
finance. This involves addressing physical risks from 
extreme weather events, transition risks associated with 
the shift to a low-carbon economy, reputational risks, 
and regulatory risks from increased climate regulations.
On the opportunity side, AAIB plans to expand its 
portfolio of sustainable finance products, such as green 
bonds and renewable energy financing, and develop 
specialized risk management services. Investing in 
innovative technologies for climate change mitigation 
and improving corporate governance by integrating 
E&S considerations are also key priorities.
The potential positive impacts include reducing carbon 
emissions through renewable energy financing, 
supporting SMEs to enhance economic resilience, and 
investing in community resilience projects. However, 
there are potential negative impacts, such as increased 
risks in sectors vulnerable to climate change, higher 
non-performing assets due to climate-related disasters, 
and operational disruptions from extreme weather 
events.

Expanding Financial Inclusion
Promoting financial inclusion (FI) is a top priority for AAIB, following the guidelines set by CBE. We aim to bring unbanked individuals and groups into the formal economy by offering customized 
solutions and services tailored to their needs, thereby integrating them into the banking sector.
AAIB introduced the Business Banking segment within the consumer banking division, catering specifically to non-borrowing companies. This strategic move is designed to diversify our portfolio, 
relying more on cost-effective funding, thus expanding our customer base and bolstering profitability. Since its inception, portfolio acquisition has increased by 6% by the start of 2023.
AAIB has taken significant steps to advance financial inclusion through a diverse portfolio of products and services tailored to meet the needs of prioritized customers. With a focus on innovation, 
AAIB offers three specialized products: simplified KYC (SKYC), no-fee savings accounts for Individuals, Micro-Corporates, and economic activity segments with no minimum balance requirements 
designed to facilitate access and usage.
This year, 822 employees received training in financial inclusion, responsible credit, and financial health, enhancing their ability to support these initiatives.
AAIB has established three active partnerships to achieve financial health and inclusion targets, collaborating with banking agents to acquire prepaid card customers.

Investing in Talent: AAIB’s High Potentials Program (HiPo)
The High Potentials (HiPo) program at AAIB is designed to improve the capacities of our most promising talents, ensuring the development of current 
and future leaders critical to AAIB’s success and strategic vision. The program aims to provide a competitive advantage by creating “success profiles” 
for various positions within the bank, thereby helping to retain top talent. It begins with an assessment center, where participants undergo tailored 
exercises, including simulations, interviews, and online assessments, to evaluate their fit for the required roles. A panel observes and assesses the 
candidates, providing individual reports on their performance and outcomes.
In 2023, we successfully assessed 95 candidates, divided into two talent pools: Senior Talents with more than ten years of experience and Junior Talents 
with 5 to 10 years of experience. From these, 54 candidates passed all assessment phases, including 39 seniors and 15 junior talents. These successful 
candidates engaged in various development opportunities, such as participating in cross-functional courses through the NTA Talent Management 
Development Program. This program covered topics like Project Management, Design Thinking, Official Ceremonies Etiquette, and Egypt’s National 
Projects and Sustainable Development Goals. They also benefited from networking opportunities, which helped them develop communication skills

Environmental Stewardship
Climate Action
As a founding signatory of the PRB and in alignment with Egypt Vision 2030, the UN SDGs, and the Paris Climate Agreement, AAIB is steadfast in its commitment to climate action. 
We recognize the critical role financial institutions play in addressing environmental challenges. By integrating sustainable practices into our operations and supporting green finance 
initiatives, we aim to reduce our carbon footprint and promote environmental stewardship. Our dedication to climate action reflects our broader mission to foster a sustainable and 
resilient future for our communities and the global ecosystem.
In 2023, AAIB conducted its operational carbon footprint assessment, demonstrating its commitment to sustainability and environmental responsibility. This assessment, prepared in 
accordance with the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol, aimed to provide a preliminary understanding of the Bank’s environmental performance. Covering 107 branches and facilities 
over an area of 173,911 square meters and including 3,090 employees, the evaluation encompassed scopes 1 and 2.

Looking Ahead: From Assessment to Action
AAIB has started by assessing its operational carbon footprint, an important step towards understanding and mitigating its environmental impact. This process evaluated emissions 
from the Bank’s direct operations covering Scopes 1 and 2. 
Looking ahead, AAIB is working on assessing its indirect Scope 3 emissions, including emissions associated with its lending portfolio, and is committed to disclosing the results in 
upcoming reports. Following this assessment, AAIB will aim to set GHG reduction targets and develop a Bank-wide decarbonization action plan to meet its targets. By disclosing the 
results in the coming years, AAIB is committed to transparency, accountability, and environmental responsibility to keep the Bank’s stakeholders informed about its environmental 
impact and progress in reducing it.

Energy Management
In 2023, AAIB’s total energy consumption amounted 
to 22,044 MWh. This primarily included 17,987 MWh of 
purchased electricity, along with 935 MWh for purchased 
chilled water, 80,696 liters of petrol for the Bank’s 
vehicles, 6,202 liters of diesel for the Bank’s vehicles, 
and 231,700 liters of diesel for the Bank’s emergency 
generators. AAIB has implemented various measures to 
enhance energy management and efficiency across its 
buildings. This includes the installation of solar panels 
on the roofs of two buildings to reduce electricity 
consumption. Additionally, the utilization of Variable 
Refrigerant Volume (VRV) technology in five buildings 
allows for automatic adjustment of cooling gas volume 
based on occupancy, ensuring energy is conserved 
when spaces are unoccupied. Moreover, the use of

Waste Management
At AAIB, waste management practices are designed to 
promote environmental sustainability and responsible 
disposal. Currently, waste separation is not conducted 
within the Bank’s premises; instead, waste collection 
contractors separate the waste at their facilities or 
public landfills according to standard procedures for 
recycling and utilization. However, a targeted plan is to 
implement waste separation at the source within the 
main headquarters buildings. This plan will be executed 
upon transitioning to the new headquarters buildings in 
New Cairo and the Administrative Capital. A trial of waste 
separation at the source has already commenced at one 
of the main headquarters buildings on Khalil Agha Street 
approximately two years ago and continues to this day.

Enhancing Operational Resilience
AAIB is bolstering its operational resilience through strategic 
infrastructure enhancements across its network. The 
construction of our Headquarters, covering an expansive area of 
47,542 square meters, establishes AAIB as a prominent presence 
in the New Administrative Capital. Utilizing cutting-edge 
technologies in building management, energy efficiency, waste 
management, and indoor environmental quality, this facility is 
designed as a Green Building, complete with solar panels to 
promote sustainability. Scheduled for occupancy by 2025, it will 
provide optimized working spaces for our employees, fostering 
a conducive environment for productivity. Simultaneously, our 
Disaster Recovery Site in 6th of October has been upgraded 
with a Building Management System technology, ensuring 
real-time monitoring of operations and bolstering reliability. 
In addition to opening two smart and energy-efficient new 
branches in 2023, we have upgraded infrastructure across our 
existing branches, replacing HVAC systems in 15 branches and 
installing additional UPS units for security systems coverage.

Developing Our LEED Gold Headquarters
AAIB is making significant progress in its sustainability journey with the development of our 
environmentally conscious headquarters. This modern facility, designed to reflect our commitment 
to environmental stewardship, aims to be a key milestone in our sustainability efforts. We are 
working towards achieving LEED Gold certification, aspiring to join the select few buildings in 
Egypt that meet such high sustainability standards. Spanning a total built-up area of 52,500 
square meters, the headquarters is designed to incorporate advanced technologies in building 
management, energy efficiency, waste management, and indoor environmental quality. Our data 
center, planned with top-tier infrastructure technologies and redundancy, is targeting a “Tier” 
certification to ensure operational reliability. Scheduled for completion in 2025, this headquarters 
will seek to provide AAIB employees with a high-quality working environment, enhancing 
productivity and well-being.

Pillar Definition
Health
The Bank shall only include in this pillar the projects that belong to the health sector establishments such as hospitals, clinics (excluding cosmetic clinics), 
laboratories, radiology and analysis centers, etc. Or institutions that serve that sector, such as institutions that manufacture medical devices, equipment, and 
prosthetic devices, except merchants. In the case of financing suppliers, only those who supply products specifically related to the health sector, such as medical 
devices and equipment, medicines, and medical supplies, are included in this pillar, but suppliers of adaptations, for example, who work with other sectors, even 
in the case of supplying to hospitals are not included in this pillar. 
Education
The Bank shall only include in this pillar projects that support the education system and increase its efficiency, such as schools, universities, institutes, teacher 
development institutions, and institutions that serve this sector, such as companies that supply school supplies and school tools. In the case of financing con -

CBE Environmental Pillars
Pillar Definition
Water
The Bank shall include only in the pillar of water the water projects with an environmental dimension aiming at preserving and treating water, removing chem-
ical and biological pollutants, and protecting freshwater ecosystems. This pillar does not include providing water for public use. Environmental water projects 
include, for example, improving water efficiency and quality, treating wastewater and sewer networks, desalinating seawater or groundwater to produce fresh 
water, collecting and purifying water, and purifying waterways.
Sustainable 
Transportation
The sustainable transportation dimension includes financing transportation projects that depend partially or completely on clean energy and reduce depend-
ence on fossil fuels, such as metro/electric trains, electric cars, and hybrid transportation (hybrid transportation combines a conventional fuel engine with an 
electric motor, which leads to burning less fuel).
Green products
and materials
The Bank shall include in the pillar green products and materials the projects that manufacture green products and materials that are less harmful to the envi-
ronment than other products that serve the same purpose and products whose manufacture, disposal, and other steps in their life cycle are less harmful to the 
environment. This is in addition to projects that use these products as raw materials and sustainable packaging lines. Green products and materials include, for

example, organic products, eco-labeled products, and biodegradable products.
Adaptation
The adaptation pillar includes projects to adapt to climate change and mitigate or avoid its damages, such as projects to build sea walls to prevent damage from 
sea level rise, projects to confront coastal erosion, projects to raise the efficiency of infrastructure to withstand potential climate changes, and projects aimed 
at reducing water use and recycling it due to drought. It also includes financing companies that work to shift from traditional practices that cause emissions to 
more sustainable ones.
Climate-smart 
agriculture (CSA)
The Bank shall only include in this pillar the projects that rely on climate-smart agriculture methods and mechanisms aiming to reduce agricultural sector emis-
sions and waste of resources by changing the sector’s conventional practices to include reliance on ecosystem services to support production, adaptation, and 
climate change mitigation and rationalize resource consumption other than the agriculture projects in general. The CSA pillar includes adaptive crop cultivation 
projects, those that rely on modern sustainable irrigation methods reducing water waste such as sprinkler or drip irrigation. These methods will lead to improved 
pest, water, and nutrient management, degraded land rehabilitation projects, and improved use of water and nitrogen fertilizer and fertilization management.

This is the second progress report of the Arab African international Bank (defined as “AAIB”, 
“the Bank”, or “We”) on its implementation of the United Nations Environment Programme 
Finance Initiative’s (UNEP-FI) Principles for Responsible Banking (PRB, the Principles). 
AAIB along with 129 other international banks became a founding signatory of the Principles in 
2019, to strengthen their contribution and align their business strategies with the UN 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Paris Climate Agreement.  
Reporting Period
The report indicates AAIB’s progress on the Six UNEP-FI Principles covering the period for the 
fiscal year 2022. Some Information before and after these dates may be included to emphasize 
relevant context to the reporting period. 
In consideration of the environment, our report is published, as a downloadable PDF file from 
our website.
Scope of the Report
The Report highlights AAIB’s remarkable footsteps and progress towards aligning with key 
frameworks including; the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC), the Equator Principles (EP), 
and the UNEP-FI to enhance and guide its business activities. 
Throughout this report, we will present how we addressed our stakeholders’ material topics 
and enhanced our sustainability performance, as well as the Bank’s approach to national, 
regional & global risks, challenges, and opportunities.

Reflecting on 2022 and the preceding years, the world has navigated through a prolonged 
period dominated by global uncertainty and unrelenting economic headwinds, curtailing the 
growth of industries and the wellbeing of communities at large.
As we witness businesses stabilizing and progressing, we believe that corporations are being 
held to a higher standard than ever before to address the ever-growing challenges and needs 
of the community and environment beyond their walls ― a commitment that I am proud to 
say we have upheld as an organization throughout the years.
Our journey with sustainability started in 2003 with our ambitious business growth strategy 
― with that growth came the realization that we need to rise to higher levels of corporate 
citizenship based on our capacity and ability to create value, making socioeconomic impact 
part of our daily operations. Our determination to achieve sustainable growth and act as a 
catalyst for positive change became a mission beyond banking as AAIB was one of the leading 
banks to set up the foundations of sustainable finance and one of the first banks to develop a

Treasury and Capital Market
The Treasury and Capital Market Group at AAIB oversees the management of liquidity and 
market risks associated with the Bank's balance sheet. It also offers expert advisory and trading 
services to AAIB's clients in global markets. The group’s main activities include trading in 
government debt instruments, trading in foreign exchange, money markets, financial 
derivatives, and hedge products, as well as managing the Bank’s liquidity, product development, 
and market research.
Investment Group
The Investment Group has made significant investments to support its activities and strategic 
direction. This includes seizing new investment opportunities by investing in existing enterprises 
to mitigate risk and earn faster revenues. Additionally, the Bank has five subsidiaries; Arab 
African Investment Management (AAIM), Arab African International Securities (AAIS), Arab 
African International Mortgage Finance (AAIMF), Arab African International Leasing (AAIL) and 
Sandah for Microfinance. 
Financial Institutions and International Financial Services

have grown the Bank’s market share significantly over the years.

• Main International Frameworks We support
Our sustainability  performance  has been assessed by major sustainability rating frameworks. 
We use these assessments as guidelines to improve our future decisions, businesses, and 
operations. In addition, these assessments along with  our rankings and ratings compared  to 
our local and international peers serve as a benchmark clarifying where We stand.   
Since 2005, We have been forerunners opting to several international frameworks  to  assess 
our  practices.  AAIB is a signatory  to  the  UN Global Compact  (UNGC) which acts as the 
guideline for human rights, labor rights, environment, and anti-corruption; the Equator 
Principles which act as the main guideline for determining, assessing and managing social and 
environmental risks in project-related transactions and the United Nations Environmental 
Programmme Finance Initiative (UNEP FI) under which AAIB collaborated with 29 banks 
around the globe to introduce the Principles for Responsible Banking (PRBs). 
The PRBs delineate the banking  sector’s  roles and opportunities  in pursuing  national  and  
global  goals  articulated  by  Egypt  Vision  2030,  the Sustainable Development Goals, and the 
Paris Climate Agreement.

BUILDING
ON A STRONG 
FOUNDATION
To our clients, business partners, and shareholders,
On behalf of the Board of Directors, I am pleased 
to report that in 2022, AAIB made significant 
visible advances in its transformation agenda, 
strengthened its market position, and delivered 
solid financial results.
 h
A Challenging Year Worldwide
The rapidly evolving 2022 business environment 
posed challenges to businesses across sectors 
worldwide.  Rising interest rates, accelerating 
inflation, the outbreak of war between Russia and 
Ukraine, ongoing recovery from the acute impacts 
of the pandemic, and capital flows out of emerging 
markets intersected to create demanding 
conditions.  These stressors were particularly acute 
in AAIB home market, where annualized inflation 
rose from single digits at the start of the year to 
more than 20% by year-end.  To throttle back the 
pace of price increases, the Central Bank of Egypt 
(CBE) raised interest rates by a total of 800 basis 
points in 2022.  
 h
Solid Financial Position 
AAIB demonstrated resilience in navigating the 
challenges of 2022. Our profile as a dollar-based 
bank with ample reserves equips us with a valuable 
buffer against shifting conditions. Our substantial 
equity cushion empowered us to continue lending 
operations without hesitation. With our $2.2 billion 
in shareholders’ equity set against liabilities of $11 
billion, AAIB surpassed this requirement. The year 
concluded on a high note with AAIB recording a

 h
Capital Adequacy and Resilience
Our commitment to maintaining a strong capital base 
is reflected in our Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR), 
which stood at an impressive 19.49% in 2021 and 
increased to 21.53% in 2022. This upward movement 
signifies not just compliance with regulatory 
demands, but a considerable surplus that showcases 
AAIB's financial durability and prudent management. 
By strategically aligning our bank's capital with our 
risk profile, we've solidified our stance as a resilient 
pillar in the face of global financial shifts, instilling 
unwavering trust among our clients and stakeholders.
 h
Operational Highlights 
2022 was a breakthrough year for AAIB’s 
transformation agenda.  After painstakingly laying 
the foundation for change over the past several 
years, we delivered new retail solutions that are 
improving how our customers interact with their 
bank. Our revamped service and value proposition 
attracted new clients, with our total customer base 
growing by 21%.
Operational successes were not limited to our 
consumer banking division. Innovating to develop 
new financing solutions that expand the sources 
of capital available to corporate customers in our 
home market, delivering a comprehensive trade 
finance solution, establishing a reputation as a key

AAIB has a decades-long history of trailblazing. 
In recent years, we have channeled our energy

that emphasizes financial resilience, customer 
centricity, and agility.  
The Board of Directors continues to support the 
values that took root in our institution which led to 
tremendous transformations. We are confident in 
our strategy, pleased by its initial tangible results, 
and look forward to a year ahead in which we will 
demonstrate further progress that continues to

However, our commitment to driving success for our 
customers, shareholders, and the communities we

B. Classification of financial assets and financial liabilities
At initial recognition, financial assets are classified and measured according to amortized cost, fair value through 
other comprehensive income (FVTOCI) and fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). 
The financial assets are classified according to how they are managed (the Bank’s business model) and their 
contractual cash flow characteristics.
B/1 Financial assets are measured at amortized cost if the following two conditions are met and it is not 
measured at fair value through profit or loss and:
• The management intented to maintain the asset to collect contractual cashflows and;
• This contractual condition of financial assets will build cashflows in certain dates which are Solely Payments 
of Principle and Interest (SPPI).
B/2 Debt instruments have been measured at fair value through other comprehensive income “FVTOCI” if it is 
not measured at fair value through profit or loss and the following two conditions are met:
• The management intented to maintain the asset to collect contractual cash flow and/or sale of the financial 
asset;

through other comprehensive income (FVTOCI) or fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL).
At initial recognition of investment in securities that are not held for trading, the bank may choose irrevocably 
to measure the subsequent changes in securities fair value through Other comprehensive income statement. All 
other financial assets are classified at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL)
Business model assessment
The Bank assesses the objective of a business model in which a financial asset is held at the portfolio level 
because this reflects the best way the business is managed and information is presented to management. The 
information considered includes:

because this reflects the best way the business is managed and information is presented to management. The 
information considered includes:
• The stated policies and objectives for the portfolio and the operation of those policies in practice, specially 
to know whether these management policies concentrate to gain the contractual interest or reconcile 
financial assets with financial liabilities which finances these assets or target cash flow from selling the 
assets;
• How the performance of the portfolio is evaluated and reported to the Bank's management;
• The risks affecting the performance of the business model and the financial assets held within that business 
model and how these risks are managed;
• The frequency, volume and timing of sales in prior periods, the reasons for such sales and its expectations 
about future sales activity. Moreover, the bank doesn’t focus only on information related to sales activity 
separately, but also takes into consideration an overall assessment on how achieving the goal that was 
announced by the bank to manage financial assets and how to achieve cash flow.
Financial assets that are held for trading and whose performance is evaluated on a fair value basis are measured 
at fair value through profit or loss because they are neither held to collect contractual cash flows nor held both 
to collect contractual cash flows and or sell the financial assets.

Assessment of whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest 
(SPPI TEST).
For the purposes of this assessment, “principal” is defined as the fair value of the financial asset at initial 
recognition. ‘Interest’ is defined as a consideration for the time value of money and for the credit risk associated 
with the principal amount outstanding during a particular period of time and for other basic lending risks and 
costs (e.g. liquidity risk and administrative costs), as well as profit margin.
In assessing whether the contractual cashflows are solely payments of principal and interest, the bank considers 
the contractual terms of the instrument. This includes assessing whether the financial asset contains a contractual 
term that could change the timing or amount of contractual cashflows such that it would not meet this condition.

The Bank applies three stages to measure expected credit losses on financial assets that are recognized at 
amortized cost and debt instruments that are recognized at fair value through other comprehensive income. 
The financial assets can transfer between these  three stages according to changes in credit quality since initial 
recognition.
Stage 1
12 months Expected Credit Loss:
It includes financial assets on initial recognition and that do not have a significant increase in credit risk since 
the initial recognition or that have low credit risk. For these assets, expected credit loss is recognized on the 
gross carrying amount of the asset based on the expected credit losses that result from default events that are 
possible within 12 months after the reporting date.
Stage 2
Lifetime Expected Credit Loss - not credit impaired:
It includes financial assets that have a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition but that do not 
have objective evidence of impairment. For these assets, lifetime expected credit losses are recognized, but

Purchase method of accounting has been applied to all the acquisition operations. The cost of acquisition is 
measured at fair value or through the assets offered and/or equity securities issued and/or liabilities incurred 
and/or liabilities accepted on behalf of the acquired company, at the date of the exchange, plus costs directly 
attributed to the acquisition. Identifiable assets acquired, and liabilities and contingent liabilities assumed in a 
business combination are measured initially at fair values at the acquisition date, irrespective of the extent of 
any minority interest. The excess of acquisition cost over the fair value of the bank’s share of the identifiable net 
assets acquired is recorded as Goodwill. If the cost of acquisition is less than the fair value of the net assets of 
the entity acquired, the difference is recognized directly in the income statement into other operating income 
(expenses).

for using the cost method on the separate financial statements. According to the cost method; investments are 
recognized at acquisition cost plus any goodwill or less any impairment losses in value-if any-. Dividends are

D. Segment reporting
An operating segment is a group of assets and operations providing products or services whose risks and

geographical segment provides products or services within a specific economic environment characterized by 
risks and benefits different from those related to other geographical segments operating in a different economic 
environment.

at the balance sheet date are translated at the exchange rates prevailing at that date.  Foreign exchange gains 
and losses resulting from the settlement of such transactions are recognized in the following items in the income 
statement:

E. Financial assets
Financial assets classified as: Amortized cost, Fair value through other comprehensive income (FVTOCI) or 
Fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). The classification depends on the business model that manages the 
financial assets and its contractual cash flow 
F/1 Financial assets classified as amortized cost
The financial asset is retained in the business model of financial assets  held to collect contractual cash flow.
• The objective from this business model is to collect contractual cash flow which represented in principal 
and interest.
• The sale is an exceptional event for this model and under the terms of the standard represented in following:
• Significant deterioration for the issuer of financial instrument;
• Lowest sales in terms of rotation and value;

market deals, or the revaluation methods such as the Discounted Cashflow module and the Options pricing 
module, as appropriate. Derivatives are carried as financial assets when its fair value is positive and as financial 
liabilities when its fair value is negative.

H. Fees and commission income
Fees charged for servicing a loan or facility that is measured at amortized cost, are recognized as revenue as 
the service is provided. Fees and commissions on non-performing or impaired loans or receivables cease to 
be recognized as income and are rather recorded off-balance sheet. These are recognized as revenue - on a 
cash basis - only when interest income on those loans is recognized in profit or loss, at which time, fees and 
commissions that are an integral part of the effective interest rate of a financial asset are treated as an adjustment 
to the effective interest rate of that financial asset.
Commitment fees received by the bank to originate a loan are deferred if it is probable to be draw down and 
are regarded as a compensation for an ongoing involvement with the acquisition of the financial instrument and 
recognized as an adjustment to the effective interest rate of the loan and in case of the commitment period has 
expired without issuing the loan, fees and commission are considered as income at the end of the commitment 
period.
Fees related to debt instruments is measured by fair value and recognized as profit, Loan syndication fees are 
recognized as revenue when the syndication has been completed and the bank has retained no part of the loan 
package for itself or has retained a part at the same effective interest rate as the other participants.

Impairment of non-financial assets
Assets that do not have definite useful lives - except for goodwill - are not amortized, and are tested annually

The income tax on the bank’s period profits or losses including both current tax, and deferred income tax is 
recognized in the income statement, except when it relates to items directly recognized into equity, in which case 
the tax is also recognized directly in equity. Income tax is calculated on the taxable profits using the prevailing 
tax rates as of balance sheet in addition to tax adjustments for previous Period.  
Deferred income tax is provided on temporary differences arising between the tax bases of assets and liabilities 
and their carrying amounts in the financial statements.  Deferred tax is determined based on the method used to 
realize or settle the current values of these assets and liabilities, using the tax rates prevailing as of the balance 
sheet date. 
Deferred tax assets are recognized when there is a reasonable probability that future taxable profits will be 
realized through which the asset can be utilized. Deferred tax assets are reduced by the portion that will not be

3.A. Credit risk
The bank is exposed to credit risk, which is the risk that a party will fail to fulfill its contractual obligations. The 
credit risk is the most important risk to the bank, and thus management carefully manages exposure to that risk. 
Credit risk is mainly presented through lending activities that result in loans, facilities and investment activities 
that result in including debt instruments in the bank’s assets. Credit risk is also found in off-balance sheet 
financial instruments such as loan commitments. The credit risk management and control operations of the 
Credit Risk Management Group are concentrated in the Credit and Risk Management Department, which reports 
to the Board of Directors, senior management, and heads of activity units on a regular basis.
3.A.1. Credit risk measurement
3.A.1.1. Loans and advances to banks and customers

• Probability of default – by the client or counterparty on its contractual obligations.

Exposure at default is based on the amounts the bank expects to be outstanding at the time of default. For 
example, for a loan this is the face value. For a commitment, the bank includes any amount already drawn plus 
the further amount that may have been drawn by the time of default, if it occurred.
Loss given default or loss severity represents the bank’s expectation of the extent of loss on a claim should default 
occur. It is expressed as a percentage of loss per unit of exposure and typically varies by type of counterparty, 
type and seniority of claim and availability of collateral or other credit mitigation methods.
3.A.1.2. Debt securities and treasury bills
For debt securities and treasury bills external rating such as (Standard & Poor’s) rating or their equivalents are 
used by the bank for managing of the credit risk exposures. In case such ratings are unavailable, internal rating 
methods are used that are similar to those used for credit customers. The investment in those securities and bills 
are viewed as a way to gain a better credit quality mapping and maintain a readily available source to meet the 
funding requirements at the same time.
3.A.2. Risk limit control and mitigation policies
The bank manages, limits, and controls concentrations of credit risk wherever they are identified – in particular - 
to individual counterparties, groups and to industries and countries.

The bank structures the levels of credit risk it undertakes by placing limits on the amount of risk accepted in 
relation to one borrower, or group of borrowers, and to geographical and industry segments. Such risks are 
monitored on a revolving basis and subject to an annual or more frequent review, when considered necessary. 
Limits on the level of credit risk by product, industry sector, and by country are approved quarterly by the Board 
of Directors.
The exposure to any one borrower including banks is further divided by sub-limits covering on- and off-balance 
sheet exposures, and daily risk limits in relation to trading items such as forward foreign exchange contracts. 
Actual exposures against limits are monitored daily.
Exposure to credit risk is also managed through regular analysis of the ability of the borrowers and potential 
borrowers to meet interest and capital repayment obligation and by changing these lending limits when 
appropriate.

The bank employs a range of policies and practices to mitigate credit risk. The most traditional of these is 
maintaining collaterals against funds advances, which is common practice. The bank implements guidelines on 
the acceptability of specific classes of collateral or credit risk mitigation. The principal collateral types for loans 
and advances are:

3.A.2.3. Master Netting  Arrangements
The bank further restricts its exposure to credit losses by entering into master netting arrangements with 
counterparties with which it undertakes a significant volume of transactions. Master netting arrangements do not 
generally result in an offset of assets and liabilities shown in the balance sheet, as transactions are either usually 
settled on a gross basis. However, the credit risk associated with favourable contracts is reduced by a master

netting arrangement to the extent that if a default occurs, all amounts with the counterparty are terminated

3.A.2.4. Credit Related Commitments 
The primary purpose of these instruments is to ensure that funds are available to a customer as required. 
Guarantees and standby letters of credit carry the same credit risk as loans. Documentary and commercial 
letters of credit – which are written undertakings by the bank on behalf of a customer authorizing a third party 
to draw drafts on the bank up to a stipulated amount under specific terms and conditions – are collateralized by 
the underlying shipments of goods to which they relate and therefore carry less risk than a direct loan.
Commitments to extend credit represent unused portions of authorizations to extend credit in the form of 
loans, guarantees or letters of credit. With respect to credit risk on commitments to extend credit, the bank is 
potentially exposed to loss in an amount equal to the total unused commitments. However, the likely amount 
of loss is less than the total unused commitments, as most commitments to extend credit are contingent upon

Liquidity risk management process
The bank liquidity management process, as carried out within the bank and monitored by assets and liability 
committee, includes:
• Day-to-day funding, managed by monitoring future cash flows to ensure that requirements can be met. 
This includes replenishment of funds as they mature or borrowed by customers. The bank maintains an 
active presence in global money markets to ensure this to happen.
• Maintaining a portfolio of highly marketable assets that can easily be liquidated as protection against any 
unforeseen interruption to cashflow.
• Monitoring the liquidity ratios against internal and regulatory requirements by the Central Bank of Egypt.
• Managing the concentration and profile of debt maturities. 
Monitoring and reporting take the form of cash flow measurement and projections for the next day, week and 
month respectively, as these are key Periods for liquidity management. The starting point for those projections is 
an analysis of the contractual maturity of the financial liabilities and the expected collection date of the financial 
assets.
Assets and liability management also monitors unmatched medium-term assets, the level and type of undrawn 
lending commitments, the usage of overdraft facilities and the impact of contingent liabilities such as standby 
letters of credit and guarantees.

B. Capital management
The bank’s objectives when managing capital, which is a broader concept than the ‘equity’ on the face of the 
statement of financial position, are:
• To comply with the capital requirements set by Arab Republic of Egypt and countries in which bank 
branches operate.
• To safeguard the bank’s ability to continue as a going concern so that it can continue to provide returns for 
shareholders and benefits for other stakeholders.
• To maintain a strong capital base to support the development of its business.

weighed with market, credit, and operational risk as capital requirement.

74.A. Impairment losses on loans and advances
The bank reviews its loan portfolios to assess impairment at least on a quarterly basis. In determining whether an 
impairment loss should be recorded in the income statement, the bank makes judgments as to whether there is 
any observable data indicating an impairment trigger followed by measurable decrease in the estimated future 
cash flows from a portfolio of loans before the decrease can be identified with that portfolio. This evidence may 
include observable data indicating that there has been an adverse change in the payment status of borrowers in 
a group, or national or local economic conditions that correlate with defaults on assets in the bank. Management 
uses estimates based on historical loss experience for assets with credit risk characteristics and objective 
evidence of impairment similar to those in the portfolio when scheduling its future cash flows. The method and 
assumptions used to estimate the amount and the timing of future cash flows are reviewed on a regular basis in 
order to reduce any difference between the expected and the actual loss based on experience

B. Impairment of equity investments through other comprehensive income
The bank determines that available-for-sale equity investments are impaired when there has been a significant or 
prolonged decline in the fair value below its cost. This determination of whether they are significant or prolonged 
requires judgment. In making this judgment, the bank evaluates among other factors, the volatility in share price. 
In addition, objective evidence of impairment may be deterioration in the financial health of the investee, industry 
and sector performance, changes in technology, and operational and financing cash flows.
C. Fair value of Derivatives
The fair values of financial instruments where no active market exists or where quoted prices are not otherwise 
available are determined by using valuation techniques. In these cases, the fair values are estimated from 
observable data in respect of similar financial instruments or using models. Where market observable inputs are 
not available, they are estimated based on appropriate assumptions. Where valuation techniques (for example, 
models) are used to determine fair values, they are validated and Periodically reviewed by qualified personnel 
independent of those that sourced them. All models are certified before they are used, and models are calibrated

independent of those that sourced them. All models are certified before they are used, and models are calibrated 
to ensure that outputs reflect actual data and comparative market prices. To the extent practical, models use 
only observable data; however, areas such as credit risk (both own credit risk and counterparty risk), volatilities 
and correlations require management to make estimates. Changes in assumptions about these factors could 
affect the reported fair value of financial instruments.
D. Amortized cost investments 
The bank classifies some non-derivative financial assets with fixed or determinable payments and fixed maturity 
as held to maturity. This classification requires significant judgment. In making this judgment, the bank evaluates 
its intention and ability to hold such investments to maturity. If the bank were to fail to keep these investments 
until maturity other than for the specific circumstances – for example, selling an insignificant amount close to 
maturity – the bank is required to reclassify the entire category as available for sale. Accordingly, the investments 
would be measured at fair value instead of amortized cost, in addition to suspending the classification of any 
investments in this category.

21. Derivatives    
Currency forwards represent commitments to purchase foreign and domestic currency, including undelivered 
spot transactions.  Foreign currency and interest rate futures are contractual obligations to receive or pay a net 
amount based on changes in currency rates or interest rates, or to buy or sell foreign currency or a financial 
instrument on a future date at a specified price, established in an active financial market.

instrument on a future date at a specified price, established in an active financial market. 
Credit risk is considered low, and future interest rate contract represents future exchange rate contracts 
negotiated for case by case, These contracts require financial settlements of any differences in contractual 
interest rates and prevailing market interest rates on future interest rates on future dates based on contractual 
amount (nominal value) pre agreed upon.
Forward rate agreements are individually negotiated interest rate futures that call for a cash settlement at a 
future date for the difference between a contracted rate of interest and the current market rate, based on a 
notional principal amount.
Currency and interest rate swaps are commitments to exchange one set of cash flows for another. Swaps result in 
an economic exchange of currencies or interest rates (for example, fixed rate for floating rate) or a combination 
of all these (i.e., cross-currency interest rate swaps).
No exchange of principal takes place, except for certain currency swaps.  
The bank’s credit risk represents the potential cost to replace the swap contracts if counterparties fail to 
fulfill their obligation. This risk is monitored on an ongoing basis with reference to the current fair value, and a 
proportion of the notional amount of the contracts. In order to control the level of credit risk taken, the bank

The notional amounts of certain types of financial instrument provide a basis for comparison with instruments 
recognized on the balance sheet but do not necessarily indicate the amounts of future cash flows involved or the 
current fair value of the instruments and, therefore; do not indicate the bank  ’s exposure to credit or price risks. 
The derivative instruments become favorable (assets) or unfavorable (liabilities) as a result of fluctuations in 
market interest rates or foreign exchange rates relative to their terms.  The aggregate contractual or notional 
amount of derivative financial instruments on hand, the extent to which instruments are favorable or unfavorable, 
and thus the aggregate fair values of derivative financial assets and liabilities, can fluctuate significantly from 
time to time.

immediately).

approximately 30% for LCY & 108% for FCY YTD; 
similarly, AAIB has high LCR & NSFR Ratios of 
approx. 200% & 170% simultaneously.

Treasury Back
Office Operations
 
Treasury Operations plays a crucial role in settling TCM transactions and is 
integral to the TCM’s overall success. The team is dedicated to following up, 
processing, and settling trades promptly to complete the settlement process of all 
transactions. The Treasury Operations team is also pivotal in accurately keeping 
correct positions and affecting the relevant P&L.
After a trade is confirmed, the role of Treasury Operations is to keep the 
accounting records for all completed transactions ordered, maintaining a strict 
dedication to details. They work under tight deadlines, booking trades rapidly with 
maximum accuracy and integrity.
Treasury Operations monitors our correspondent bank accounts’ balances and 
provide TCM / ALM with the most accurate figures of the closing credits for the 
cash flow so that it can be invested most profitably. They also manage the daily 
cash outflow requirement, following applicable procedures, to ensure every 
request is in line with the approved policies & guidelines.
Financial Institutions & Correspondent 
Banking Relations

relationship with AAIB. The broad scope of the division’s correspondent network

SUSTAINABILITY
Principles of Responsible Banking
AAIB collaborated with the United Nations 
Environmental Program Finance Initiative (UNEP 
FI) and 29 other leaders of the global banking 
industry to establish the Principles for Responsible 
Banking (PRB). AAIB is a Founding Signatory of the 
Principles. AAIB published its first report in 2021.
Equator Principle
AAIB EP report published in 2021 AAIB 
broadened the risk management scope to include 
environmental and social (E&S) risks such as 
climate change, income inequality, and more 
constituting sources of major financial tremors 
and instability. To this end, AAIB was one of the 
first banks to recognize that banking could be 
a force for good in shaping an equitable and 
resilient society and the importance of embedding 
sustainable criteria into banking decisions. More 
than ten years ago, AAIB became the first bank 
in Egypt to subscribe to the Equator Principles 
(EP). AAIB has been taking active steps towards 
further consolidating a solid infrastructure built 
around the E&S Policy, Organizational Structure, 
and Capacity Building. The EP is recognized as 
the main guideline for determining, assessing, and 
managing E&S risks in project-related transactions.

The COVID-19 pandemic’s harmful impact on 
microfinance institutions continued during 2021.
AAIB’s activities and plans were deeply impacted 
by the global COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, making 
it difficult for AAIB to achieve its targets. Despite 
declining demand volume and postponement of 
installments, the company’s financial performance 
was relatively positive. It achieved revenues of EGP 
86 million compared to EGP 80.7 million in 2020 (an 
increase of 7%). Also, the company adopted policies 
to control expenses and achieved a relative decrease 
in general costs by 1%.
Although the waves of coronavirus receded by the 
end of 2021, economic recovery has just begun. 
And in 2022, the company will face new challenges 
posed by the Russian-Ukrainian war and its expected 
impact on the global economy. The conflict is 
starting to affect levels of inflation. High inflation 
will negatively impact our target customers in terms 
of granting new facilities on the one hand and 
maintaining the quality of the facilities portfolio on 
the other hand.
In 2021, the company implemented a new automated 
system (T24), which will help AAIB improve the level 
of services it provides to our customers. Applying 
our new automated system is an opportunity to 
advance the Bank’s digital transformation. It is also 
a chance for AAIB and Egypt to progress toward 
their goal of financial inclusion and services for all 
Egyptians.

12 months Expected Credit Loss
It includes financial assets on initial recognition

is recognized on the gross carrying amount of the

months after the reporting date.

Lifetime Expected Credit Loss - not credit impaired
It includes financial assets that have a significant 
increase in credit risk since initial recognition but 
that do not have objective evidence of impairment. 
For these assets, lifetime expected credit losses 
are recognized, but interest is still calculated on 
the gross carrying amount of the asset. Lifetime 
expected credit loss is the expected credit loss that 
results from all possible default events over the 
expected life of the financial instrument.

I. Interest income and expense
Interest income and expense on all interest-bearing 
financial instruments are recognized in “Interest 
income” and “Interest expense” line items in the 
income statement using the effective interest rate 
method, except for those classified as held for 
trading or initially classified as fair value through 
profit or loss.
The effective interest rate is a method of calculating 
the amortized cost of a financial asset or a financial 
liability and allocating its interest income or interest 
expense over the relevant period. The effective 
interest rate is the rate that exactly discounts 
estimated future cash payments or cash receipts 
through the expected life of the financial instrument 
or, when appropriate, a shorter period to the net 
carrying amount of the financial asset or financial 
liability on initial recognition. When calculating the 
effective interest rate, the bank estimates the future 
cash flows, considering all contractual terms of 
the financial instrument (for example, prepayment 
options) but does not consider future credit losses. 
The calculation includes all fees and commissions 
paid or received between parties of the contract 
which is considered an integral part of the effective 
interest rate, in addition to transaction costs and all 
other premiums or discounts.

The bank regularly reviews its risk management 
policies and systems to reflect changes in markets, 
products, and best emerging applications.
Risk management is carried out by a risk 
department under policies approved by the Board 
of Directors. Credit risk management identifies, 
evaluates and covers financial risks in close 
collaboration with the various operational units of 
the bank. The board provides written principles 
for risk management as a whole, as well as written 
policies covering specific risk areas such as credit 
risk, foreign currency risk, interest rate risk, and 
derivative and non-derivative instruments. In 
addition, credit risk management is responsible for 
periodic review of risk management and the control 
environment independently.

manages exposure to that risk. Credit risk is

A.2. Risk limit control and mitigation policies
The bank manages, limits, and controls 
concentrations of credit risk wherever they 
are identified – in particular - to individual 
counterparties, groups and to industries and 
countries.
The bank structures the levels of credit risk it 
undertakes by placing limits on the amount of risk 
accepted in relation to one borrower, or group 
of borrowers, and to geographical and industry 
segments. Such risks are monitored on a revolving 
basis and subject to an annual or more frequent 
review, when considered necessary. Limits on the 
level of credit risk by product, industry sector, and 
by country are approved quarterly by the Board of 
Directors.
The exposure to any one borrower including banks 
is further divided by sub-limits covering on- and 
off-balance sheet exposures, and daily risk limits 
in relation to trading items such as forward foreign 
exchange contracts. Actual exposures against limits 
are monitored daily.
Exposure to credit risk is also managed through 
regular analysis of the ability of the borrowers and 
potential borrowers to meet interest and capital 
repayment obligation and by changing these 
lending limits when appropriate.
