A.2.1. Collateral
The bank employs a range of policies and practices 
to mitigate credit risk. The most traditional of these 
is maintaining collaterals against funds advances, 
which is common practice. The bank implements 
guidelines on the acceptability of specific classes 
of collateral or credit risk mitigation. The principal 
collateral types for loans and advances are:
• Mortgages over residential properties.
• Pledge on business assets like machinery and 
merchandise.
• Pledge in financial instruments like debt 
instruments and equity. 
Longer-term finance and lending to corporate 
entities are generally secured; revolving individual 
credit facilities are generally unsecured. The 
Bank attempts to mitigate the credit risk through 
additional collaterals from the concerned parties 
immediately on arising of impairment indicators for 
any of the loans or facilities.
Collateral held as security for financial assets other 
than loans and advances depends on the nature 
of the instrument. Debt securities, treasury and 
other eligible bills are generally unsecured, with the 
exception of Asset-backed Securities and similar 
instruments, which are secured by portfolios of 
financial instruments.

In addition to the four credit rating levels (note 3.A.1), management classifies categories that are more 
detailed so as to agree with the requirements of the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE). Assets subject to credit 
risk are classified in these categories in accordance with regulations and detailed conditions that largely 
depend on information related to the client, his/her activity, financial position, and regularity of repayment.
The bank calculates the required provisions for the impairment of the assets subject to credit risk, including 
commitments related to credit, on the basis of ratios specified by the Central Bank of Egypt. In case the 
impairment loss provision required by the Central Bank of Egypt exceeds that required for the purpose of 
financial statement preparation in accordance with the Egyptian accounting standards, retained earnings are 
decreased to support the General Bank risk reserve with the amount of the increase. This reserve is
periodically revised for an increase or a decrease to reflect the amount of increase between the two provisions.

B/3. Interest rate risk
Cash flow interest rate risk is the risk that the future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate 
because of changes in market interest rates. Fair value interest rate risk is the risk that the value of a 
financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market interest rates. The bank takes on exposure 
to the effects of fluctuations in the prevailing levels of market interest rates on both its fair value and cash 
flow risks. Interest margins may increase because of such changes but may reduce profits in the event that

C. Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk that the bank is unable to meet its obligations associated with its financial liabilities 
when they fall due and to replace funds when they are withdrawn. The consequence may be the failure to 
meet obligation to repay depositors and fulfil commitments to lend.

Liquidity risk management process
The bank liquidity management process, as carried out within the bank and monitored by assets and 
liability committee, includes:
• Day-to-day funding, managed by monitoring future cash flows to ensure that requirements can be met. 
This includes replenishment of funds as they mature or borrowed by customers. The bank maintains an 
active presence in global money markets to ensure this to happen.
• Maintaining a portfolio of highly marketable assets that can easily be liquidated as protection against any 
unforeseen interruption to cashflow.
• Monitoring the liquidity ratios against internal and regulatory requirements by the Central Bank of Egypt.
• Managing the concentration and profile of debt maturities. 
Monitoring and reporting take the form of cash flow measurement and projections for the next day, week 
and month respectively, as these are key Periods for liquidity management. The starting point for those 
projections is an analysis of the contractual maturity of the financial liabilities and the expected collection 
date of the financial assets.

21. Derivatives    
Currency forwards represent commitments to purchase foreign and domestic currency, including 
undelivered spot transactions.  Foreign currency and interest rate futures are contractual obligations to 
receive or pay a net amount based on changes in currency rates or interest rates, or to buy or sell foreign 
currency or a financial instrument on a future date at a specified price, established in an active financial 
market. 
Credit risk is considered low, and future interest rate contract represents future exchange rate contracts 
negotiated for case by case, These contracts require financial settlements of any differences in contractual 
interest rates and prevailing market interest rates on future interest rates on future dates based on

interest rates and prevailing market interest rates on future interest rates on future dates based on 
contractual amount (nominal value) pre agreed upon.
Forward rate agreements are individually negotiated interest rate futures that call for a cash settlement at a 
future date for the difference between a contracted rate of interest and the current market rate, based on a 
notional principal amount.
Currency and interest rate swaps are commitments to exchange one set of cash flows for another.  Swaps 
result in an economic exchange of currencies or interest rates (for example, fixed rate for floating rate) or 
a combination of all these (i.e., cross-currency interest rate swaps).  No exchange of principal takes place, 
except for certain currency swaps.  
The bank’s credit risk represents the potential cost to replace the swap contracts if counterparties fail to 
fulfill their obligation. This risk is monitored on an ongoing basis with reference to the current fair value, and 
a proportion of the notional amount of the contracts. In order to control the level of credit risk taken, the 
bank assesses counterparties using the same techniques as for its lending activities.  
The notional amounts of certain types of financial instrument provide a basis for comparison with 
instruments recognized on the balance sheet but do not necessarily indicate the amounts of future cash

It is my pleasure to present to you, on behalf of myself and my fellow board members, AAIB’s 
Annual Report for the year 2016 - marking 53 years since the bank’s establishment.
I am also pleased to present you with a brief outline of the most important financial results and 
financial performance indicators for 2016, reflecting another year of the team’s exceptional 
performance and professionalism emanating from their belief in the bank’s mission and in 
adherence with its policies and strategic vision.
Below, we are pleased to present a brief on the bank’s performance: 
Net profit:
The bank achieved a net profit of USD 252 million by the end of the financial period of 
2016, compared to USD 213 million in 2015. This reflects a growth rate of 18.3% and an 
earnings per share of USD 11.8, from USD 9.8 in 2015, with a rate of return on total assets 
of 2.5% and a return on equity of 16.1%.
deposits and loans:
The year 2016 witnessed continued growth in the bank’s performance. In this regard, 
it is worth noting that the base currency used to depict AAIB’s balance sheet is the US 
dollar, which strengthened significantly against the EGP which in turn affected the bank’s 
financials. Customer deposits totaled USD 6.9 billion by the end of the year, compared to 
USD 10.7 billion in 2015 - contracting by 35% due to the impact of the changes in the FX 
rate on the bank’s EGP deposits, which actually witnessed a growth rate of 16.2%. This

Meanwhile, the bank’s total loan portfolio by the end of the financial period reached USD 
3.5 billion, compared to USD 4.7 billion the previous year, down 26% mostly due to FX rate 
dynamics. In fact, the EGP-denominated loan portfolio witnessed an actual growth rate of 
54.8% compared to a contraction of 17.6% in FC-denominated loan portfolio.  
capital base and shareholders’ equity:
Total shareholder equity at the end of the year stood at USD 1.5 billion, compared to USD 
1.3 billion the previous year with an annual capital growth rate of 14.1% - which is close to 
2015’s growth rate of 14.7%. Meanwhile, the Capital Adequacy Ratio reached 22.21% by 
end 2016, exceeding 2015’s 17.1%. It thus achieved the highest protection rates on that 
front and the ability to face growth requirements in light of future challenges. This level 
also surpassed the minimum level prescribed by the Central Bank of Egypt in light of the 
regulations and standards set by the Bank for International Settlements that amount to 
10%.
total assets:
The bank’s total assets amounted to USD 9.9 billion by the end of the financial period, 
compared to USD 13.5 billion the previous year - contracting 26.2% on the back of FX rate 
changes and the USD/EGP rate by the end of the period. It is worth mentioning that the

It is my pleasure to present to you on behalf of the board of directors a brief overview of AAIB’s 
performance and the important achievements that have been made during the financial year that 
ended December 31, 2016. I would also like to highlight the most important economic developments 
on the domestic and global levels and their impact on the finance and banking sectors. 
global economy Prospects
Despite the reduction in the size of global trade and the slump in demand afflicting the economic 
situation, there are expectations of a slight improvement in the global economy of 3.4% growth 
versus 3.1% in 2016.
The fiscal stimulus policies being implemented by the world’s major economies could result in the 
achievement of local and global growth that is faster than expected, although rising protectionism 
will also have its negative effects. It is expected that growth rates of emerging and developing 
markets will witness a revival, for a combined growth rate of 4.5% (versus 4.1% the previous 
year), with the slight increase in raw material prices. 
It is also expected that the investment outlook during 2017 will be influenced by a number of 
factors, topped by the new American administration, stabilization in crude oil prices, progress on 
Brexit negotiations, in addition to the US Federal Reserve’s rate hike to the levels of 1.31.5%- by 
yearend - making three consecutive increases in US interest rates.

yearend - making three consecutive increases in US interest rates. 
The year of 2016 witnessed a situation characterized by numerous reductions in oil prices and 
revenues from global bonds. Much of this is expected to reverse during this year. There are a 
number of growth-supporting factors in developing countries, starting with a shift from focus on 
monetary policy to concentration on fiscal policy in developed economies. 
Moreover, an expansionary economic policy in the US has pushed the Fed to tighten monetary 
policy more rapidly, which should increase US returns. This is in addition to the revival in global oil 
prices, with markets regaining balance on the back of the agreement to cut production by OPEC 
countries and strong growth in demand. 
Equity markets are also expected to overshadow other asset classes, led by US and EU markets, 
and the US dollar maintaining its position with the probability of the EUR and USD equalization. 
In regards to the MENA region, growth rates are expected to improve during the year with the 
continuation of the positive effects of economic reform, topped by the Egyptian economic reform 
program. 
local economy
The past year has seen several important developments at the local level, in the context of 
policy reforms aimed at reviving the economy, encouraging investment and capital flows, and 
strengthening foreign currency reserves. Indeed, the most important of these reforms was the

strengthening foreign currency reserves. Indeed, the most important of these reforms was the 
Central Bank of Egypt’s (CBE) decision in November to float the EGP while raising the discount 
rate and the lending and borrowing interest rates per day (Corridor) by 3% to counter inflationary 
trends following the flotation of the local currency, which fell by 100% against major currencies.
In the framework of coordination between fiscal and monetary policy, the decision to float the EGP 
and raise the basic interest rate coincided with the partial elimination of fuel subsidies and the 
application of the VAT law in September 2016 after its adoption by the House of Representatives. 
Naturally, this negatively impacted inflation, which reached 24.5% in December.
Meanwhile, these decisions had a positive impact on a number of fronts, whereby the Egyptian 
stock exchange has seen its biggest rise in eight years and foreign currency reserves increased 
to reach USD 24.26 billion at the end of December after they had fallen by half since 2011. This is 
in addition to support from international funding institutions for the reforms, whereby the Executive 
Board of the International Monetary Fund agreed to Egypt’s request for a loan of USD 12 billion 
over three years. Indeed, Egypt has already received the first tranche, consisting of USD 2.75 
billion, over two stages during the last quarter of the year.

aaiB corporate governance report – fY 2016
The common goal of AAIB’s Board, management and staff is to create sustainable value, 
to guarantee the stability and continuity of our Institution and to maximize its value in the 
medium to long term. We believe that strong leadership and good governance are key to 
achieving these goals. This conviction drives us to:
● Comply with regulatory standards, and be an “early adopter”, where appropriate, by 
complying before a published law or recommendation takes effect; and
● Remain at the forefront of international best governance practices by continuously 
benchmarking our governance framework against what the Board considers to be best 
practice internationally.
The Bank has established a strong governance framework that is designed to protect the 
interests of all stakeholders, ensure compliance with regulatory requirements, and enhance 
organizational efficiency. This framework includes a healthy organizational structure that 
clearly segregates functions and responsibilities; clear mandates for the Board and its sub-
committees, management, and management committees.

aaiB Board of directors
AAIB’s Board structure is consistent with best practice and Central Bank of Egypt directives, 
which promote the separation between the roles of the Chairman as a non-executive and 
the Executive Director of the Bank. The Bank’s Board of Directors consists of eight qualified 
members: seven non-executive directors (NEDs) including the Chairman of the Board and 
one Executive Director.
The Board is responsible for the overall stewardship of the Bank, including the establishment 
of AAIB’s strategic direction, overseeing the achievement of its long-term goals, as 
well as overseeing the effectiveness of internal controls. The Board of Directors is also 
responsible for ensuring that business activities are aligned with the interests of AAIB’s 
main stakeholders, and within the framework of governing laws and regulations and the 
Bank’s approved policies. In 2016, two new directors joined the Board, being Mr. Abdel 
Salam Al Anwar who was appointed in April to replace Dr. Hala El Said, and Ms. Lobna 
Helal, appointed in June replacing Mr. Aly Shaker. Over the course of FY 2016, AAIB’s 
Board of Directors convened seven times.

Board committees
The Board is assisted in the discharge of its responsibilities by five sub-committees: Audit 
(AC), Risk (RC), Corporate Governance (CGC), Remuneration (RemCo), and the Executive 
Committee (ExCo). All Board committees have formal well-defined terms of reference 
governing their activities, which are reviewed periodically to assess the adequacy of 
their respective charters and to ensure that they reflect regulatory requirements and best 
practices. With the exception of the RC and the ExCo, board committees consist entirely 
of non-executive directors. Committees may engage external advisors at the expense of 
AAIB to support their duties. Each committee, through its chair, reports to the Board with 
respect to its activities and with such recommendations as are deemed appropriate in the 
circumstances.
audit committee
The Audit Committee assists the Board in performing its oversight responsibilities of the 
quality and integrity of Bank’s financial statements and disclosures of the financial condition; 
the adherence to internal policies and procedures and the Bank’s compliance with legal 
and regulatory requirements.
AAIB’s Audit Committee comprises of four non-executive directors and its meetings are 
attended by the Head of Internal Audit as well as the Head of Compliance. The Committee 
met five times over the course of FY 2016.

risk committee
The main role of the Risk Committee is to assist the Board in fulfilling its oversight 
responsibilities with regards to the effectiveness of the Bank’s risk management framework, 
including the assessment of the adequacy of the Bank’s risk policies, and monitoring 
compliance therewith. The Committee consists of three non-executive directors and one 
executive director. The Head of the Risk Management Group is a permanent attendee 
of the Committee meetings. Over the course of FY 2016, the Risk Committee met four 
times.
corporate governance committee
The Corporate Governance Committee supports the Board in fulfilling its oversight 
responsibilities regarding the effectiveness of the Bank’s corporate governance framework, 
including the development of a set of corporate governance guidelines and standards 
and overseeing the Bank’s compliance therewith. The Committee is formed of four non-
executive directors. The Committee met two times during FY 2016.
remuneration committee
The Remuneration Committee assists the Board in fulfilling its responsibilities with regards 
to setting the remuneration of the Bank’s senior management and key executives, and to 
ensure that such remuneration is in line with individual, as well
as the Bank’s overall performance, and consistent with the Bank’s objectives and long-
term goals, as well as its policies, governance standards, and applicable regulations. The

internal committees

internal control functions
AAIB maintains a robust internal control framework that comprises of the following functions: 
Internal Control, Compliance, Risk Management, and Internal Audit. The control functions 
ensure that Bank operations are compliant with internal policies and relevant regulations, 
and that risk policies are current in addressing and managing the various risks to which 
AAIB is exposed.
internal control
The Internal Control Division monitors the Bank’s daily operations. Its key activity is to ensure 
that the established controls are complied with. The Internal Control Division reviews the 
daily transactions on the Bank’s ledgers to ensure their proper execution, documentation, 
and compliance with regulatory and internal regulations, policies, and guidelines. The 
Division’s role expands to the regular review of various functions at the branch level.
compliance
As Compliance is crucial to the success of our business, the main role of AAIB’s Compliance 
Function is to safeguard the Bank against “compliance risk”, which is defined as the risk of 
legal or regulatory sanctions, material financial loss, or loss to reputation a bank may suffer 
as a result of its failure to comply with compliance laws, rules and standards applicable to

The Compliance Function includes the following units:

The Department identifies and documents proactively the compliance risks associated with

internal audit and inspection
●  The mission of the Audit and Inspection Division is to provide independent, objective 
assurance and consulting services that can assist in improving AAIB>s overall activities 
and operations. This will assist the Bank to accomplish its objectives by adopting an 
objective approach to evaluate and improve the effectiveness of risk management, 
control and governance processes.
● The Audit and Inspection Division is an independent function reporting technically to 
the Audit Committee, which is constituted from Board members assigned by the Bank’s 
Board, and administratively to both the Chairman and Vice Chairman and Managing 
Director. Audit reports are presented to the Vice Chairman and Managing Director being 
the Bank’s the Chief Executive Officer, and the Audit Committee.

presentation approved by the Central Bank of Egypt on 16 December 2008, under the historical cost convention 
modified to re-evaluate financial assets and financial liabilities held for trading, financial assets and financial liabilities 
classified at inception at fair value through profits or losses and financial investments available for sale, and all

I. Interest income and expense
Interest income and expense for all interest-bearing financial instruments, except for those classified as held for 
trading or designated at fair value through profit or loss,  are recognized within ‘interest income’ and ‘interest

The effective interest method is a method of calculating the amortized cost of a financial asset or a financial liability 
and of allocating the interest income or interest expense over the relevant Period. The effective interest rate is the 
rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash payments or receipts through the expected life of the financial 
instrument or, when appropriate, a shorter Period to the net carrying amount of the financial asset or financial 
liability. When calculating the effective interest rate, the bank estimates cash flows considering all contractual 
terms of the financial instrument (for example, prepayment options) but does not consider future credit losses. The 
calculation includes all fees and points paid or received between parties to the contract that are an integral part of 
the effective interest rate, transaction costs and all other premiums or discounts.
Once a financial asset or a group of similar financial assets has been classified as nonperforming or impaired, 
related interest income is not recognized and is recorded in marginal records apart from the financial statements, 
and is recognized as revenues according to cash basis as follows:
- When they are collected, after receiving all past due instalments for consumption loans, mortgage loans, and 
small business loans.

Q. Impairment of non-financial assets
Assets that have an indefinite useful life are not subject to amortization-except goodwill- and are tested annually 
for impairment. Assets that are subject to amortization are reviewed for impairment whenever events or changes in 
circumstances indicate that the carrying amount may not be recoverable.
An impairment loss is recognized for the amount by which the asset’s carrying amount exceeds its recoverable 
amount. The recoverable amount is the higher of an asset’s fair value less costs to sell and value in use. For 
the purposes of assessing impairment, assets are grouped at the lowest levels for which there are separately 
identifiable cash flows (cash-generating units). Non-financial assets that suffered impairment are reviewed for 
possible reversal of the impairment at each reporting date.

1. Pension obligations
The bank has a special social fund scheme (the Fund) that is not subject to the general law (law 79 for 1975) as 
it was established under law 64 for 1980 and this Fund has its own alternative independent articles of insurable 
rights (Pension / Bonuses / one payment compensation) and according to the ministry decree 94 for 1985. This fund 
covers only the bank employees in the Head Quarter and branches in the Arab Republic of Egypt.
The bank is committed to pay the Fund its monthly contributions, which calculated according the Fund’s articles of

business, and the operational risks are an inevitable consequence of being in business. The bank’s aim is therefore to

Risk management is carried out by a risk department under policies approved by the Board of Directors. Financial

management, as well as written policies covering specific areas, such as foreign exchange risk, interest rate risk,

A.  Credit risk
The bank is exposed to credit risk, which is the risk of suffering financial loss, should any of the bank’s customers, 
clients or market counterparties fail to fulfill their contractual obligations to the bank. Credit risk is the most important 
risk for the bank’s business. Management therefore carefully manages its exposure to credit risk. Credit risk arises 
mainly from lending activities which resulted in loans, facilities and investment activities which result in including 
the financial assets in bank’s assets. Credit risk is available in the off-balance sheet financial assets such lending 
commitment. The credit risk management and control are centralized in a credit risk management team, which 
reports to the Board of Directors and head of each business unit regularly.

 A.2 Risk limit control and mitigation policies
The bank manages, limits and controls concentrations of credit risk wherever they are identified − in particular, to 
individual counterparties, groups and to industries and countries.
The bank structures the levels of credit risk it undertakes by placing limits on the amount of risk accepted in relation 
to one borrower, or groups of borrowers, and to geographical and industry segments. Such risks are monitored on 
a revolving basis and subject to an annual or more frequent review, when considered necessary. Limits on the level 
of credit risk by product, industry sector and by country are approved quarterly by the Board of Directors.
The exposure to any one borrower including banks and brokers is further restricted by sub-limits covering on- 
and off-balance sheet exposures, and daily delivery risk limits in relation to trading items such as forward foreign 
exchange contracts. Actual exposures against limits are monitored daily. 
Exposure to credit risk is also managed through regular analysis of the ability of the borrowers and potential borrowers 
to meet interest and capital repayment obligation and by changing these lending limits when appropriate.
Some other specific control and mitigation measures are outlined below:
• Collateral

Some other specific control and mitigation measures are outlined below:
• Collateral
The bank employs a range of policies and practices to mitigate credit risk. The most traditional of these is the taking 
of security for funds advances, which is common practice. The bank implements guidelines on the acceptability of 
specific classes of collateral or credit risk mitigation. The principal collateral types for loans and advances are:
- Mortgages over residential properties.
- Charges over business assets such as premises, inventory.
- Charges over financial instruments such as debt securities and equities.
Longer-term finance and lending to corporate entities are generally secured; revolving individual credit facilities are 
generally unsecured. In addition, in order to minimise the credit loss the bank will seek additional collateral from the 
counterparty as soon as impairment indicators are identified for the relevant individual loans and advances.
Collateral held as security for financial assets other than loans and advances depends on the nature of the 
instrument. Debt securities, treasury and other eligible bills are generally unsecured, with the exception of asset-
Backed Securities and similar instruments, which are secured by portfolios of financial instruments.
• Derivatives
The bank maintains strict control limits on net open derivative positions (i.e., the difference between purchase

inflows of instruments, which in relation to derivatives are only a fraction of the contract, or notional values used to 
express the volume of instruments outstanding. This credit risk exposure is managed as part of the overall lending 
limits with customers, together with potential exposures from market movements. Collateral or other security is not 
usually obtained for credit risk exposures on these instruments, except where the bank requires margin deposits 
from counterparties. 
Settlement risk arises in any situation where a payment in cash, securities or equities is made in the expectation of 
a corresponding receipt in cash, securities or equities. Daily settlement limits are established for each counter party 
to cover the aggregate of all settlement risk arising from the bank market’s transactions on any single day.
• Master Netting  Arrangements
The bank further restricts its exposure to credit losses by entering into master netting arrangements with counterparties 
with which it undertakes a significant volume of transactions. Master netting arrangements do not generally result in 
an offset of assets and liabilities shown in the balance sheet, as transactions are either usually settled on a gross 
basis. However, the credit risk associated with favourable contracts is reduced by a master netting arrangement to

• Credit Related Commitments 
The primary purpose of these instruments is to ensure that funds are available to a customer as required. Guarantees 
and standby letters of credit carry the same credit risk as loans. Documentary and commercial letters of credit – 
which are written undertakings by The bank on behalf of a customer authorising a third party to draw drafts on The 
bank up to a stipulated amount under specific terms and conditions – are collateralised by the underlying shipments 
of goods to which they relate and therefore carry less risk than a direct loan.
Commitments to extend credit represent unused portions of authorisations to extend credit in the form of loans, 
guarantees or letters of credit. With respect to credit risk on commitments to extend credit, the bank is potentially 
exposed to loss in an amount equal to the total unused commitments. However, the likely amount of loss is less than 
the total unused commitments, as most commitments to extend credit are contingent upon customers maintaining

Liquidity risk management process
The bank liquidity management process, as carried out within the bank and monitored by assets and liability 
committee, includes:
- Day-to-day funding, managed by monitoring future cash flows to ensure that requirements can be met. This includes 
replenishment of funds as they mature or borrowed by customers. The bank maintains an active presence in global 
money markets to enable this to happen;
- Maintaining a portfolio of highly marketable assets that can easily be liquidated as protection against any unforeseen 
interruption to cash flow;
- Monitoring the liquidity ratios against internal and regulatory requirements by the Central Bank of Egypt.
- Managing the concentration and profile of debt maturities. 
Monitoring and reporting take the form of cash flow measurement and projections for the next day, week and 
month respectively, as these are key Periods for liquidity management. The starting point for those projections is 
an analysis of the contractual maturity of the financial liabilities and the expected collection date of the financial 
assets.
Assets and Liability management also monitors unmatched medium-term assets, the level and type of undrawn 
lending commitments, the usage of overdraft facilities and the impact of contingent liabilities such as standby letters 
of credit and guarantees.

E. Capital Management
The bank’s objectives when managing capital, which is a broader concept than the ‘equity’ on the face of the 
statement of financial position, are:
- To comply with the capital requirements set by Arab Republic of Egypt and countries in which Bank branches 
operate.
- To safeguard the bank’s ability to continue as a going concern so that it can continue to provide returns for 
shareholders and benefits for other stakeholders.
- To maintain a strong capital base to support the development of its business.
- Capital adequacy and the use of regulatory capital (Central Bank of Egypt) are monitored by the bank’s management, 
employing techniques based on the guidelines developed by the Basel Committee and the European Community 
Directives, as implemented by the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) or supervisory purposes, the required information 
is filed with the Authority on a quarterly basis.
The CBE requires the bank to:
- The bank maintains a ratio of 10% or more of total regulatory capital to its risk-weighted assets and contingent 
liabilities.

4. Critical accounting estimates and judgments
The bank makes estimates and assumptions that affect the presented amounts of assets and liabilities within the next 
financial Period. Estimates and judgments are evaluated on a continuous basis, and are based on past experience 
and other factors, including expectations with regard to future events which believed to be reasonable during the 
current conditions and available information.
A. Impairment losses on loans and advances
The bank reviews its loan portfolios to assess impairment at least on a quarterly basis. In determining whether 
an impairment loss should be recorded in the income statement, the bank makes judgments as to whether there 
is any observable data indicating an impairment trigger followed by measurable decrease in the estimated future 
cash flows from a portfolio of loans before the decrease can be identified with that portfolio. This evidence may

a group, or national or local economic conditions that correlate with defaults on assets in the bank. Management 
uses estimates based on historical loss experience for assets with credit risk characteristics and objective evidence 
of impairment similar to those in the portfolio when scheduling its future cash flows. The method and assumptions 
used to estimate the amount and the timing of future cash flows are reviewed on a regular basis in order to reduce 
any difference between the expected and the actual loss based on experience
B. Impairment of available-for-sale equity investments
The bank determines that available-for-sale equity investments are impaired when there has been a significant or 
prolonged decline in the fair value below its cost. This determination of whether they are significant or prolonged 
requires judgment. In making this judgment, the bank evaluates among other factors, the volatility in share price. In 
addition, objective evidence of impairment may be deterioration in the financial health of the investee, industry and 
sector performance, changes in technology, and operational and financing cash flows.

C. Fair value of Derivatives
The fair values of financial instruments where no active market exists or where quoted prices are not otherwise 
available are determined by using valuation techniques. In these cases, the fair values are estimated from observable 
data in respect of similar financial instruments or using models. Where market observable inputs are not available, 
they are estimated based on appropriate assumptions. Where valuation techniques (for example, models) are 
used to determine fair values, they are validated and periodcally reviewed by qualified personnel independent of 
those that sourced them. All models are certified before they are used, and models are calibrated to ensure that 
outputs reflect actual data and comparative market prices. To the extent practical, models use only observable data; 
however, areas such as credit risk (both own credit risk and counterparty risk), volatilities and correlations require 
management to make estimates. Changes in assumptions about these factors could affect the reported fair value 
of financial instruments.
D. Held-to-maturity investments
The bank classifies some non-derivative financial assets with fixed or determinable payments and fixed maturity 
as held to maturity. This classification requires significant judgment. In making this judgment, the bank evaluates 
its intention and ability to hold such investments to maturity. If the bank were to fail to keep these investments to

E. Income taxes
The bank is subject to income taxes in numerous jurisdictions. Significant estimates are required in determining

whether additional taxes will be due. Where the final tax outcome of these matters is different from the amounts 
that were initially recorded, such differences will impact the income tax and deferred tax provisions in the Period 
where the differences exist.

 23. Financial Derivatives
Derivatives
- Currency forwards represent commitments to purchase foreign and domestic currency, including undelivered 
spot transactions.  Foreign currency and interest rate futures are contractual obligations to receive or pay a net 
amount based on changes in currency rates or interest rates, or to buy or sell foreign currency or a financial 
instrument on a future date at a specified price, established in an active financial market. 
- Forward rate agreements are individually negotiated interest rate futures that call for a cash settlement at a 
future date for the difference between a contracted rate of interest and the current market rate, based on a 
notional principal amount.

chunk_text:

- Currency and interest rate swaps are commitments to exchange one set of cash flows for another.  Swaps 
result in an economic exchange of currencies or interest rates (for example, fixed rate for floating rate) or a 
combination of all these (i.e., cross-currency interest rate swaps).  No exchange of principal takes place, except 
for certain currency swaps.  
- The bank’s credit risk represents the potential cost to replace the swap contracts if counterparties fail to fulfill their 
obligation. This risk is monitored on an ongoing basis with reference to the current fair value, and a proportion of 
the notional amount of the contracts.  To control the level of credit risk taken, the bank assesses counterparties 
using the same techniques as for its lending activities.  
- The notional amounts of certain types of financial instrument provide a basis for comparison with instruments 
recognized on the balance sheet but do not necessarily indicate the amounts of future cash flows involved or 
the current fair value of the instruments and, therefore, do not indicate the bank  ’s exposure to credit or price 
risks. 
- The derivative instruments become favorable (assets) or unfavorable (liabilities) as a result of fluctuations in 
market interest rates or foreign exchange rates relative to their terms.  The aggregate contractual or notional 
amount of derivative financial instruments on hand, the extent to which instruments are favorable or unfavorable,

The Department of Social Fund for employees  in the Arab African International Bank to conduct an actuarial study 
to determine the net present value of the obligations of the Fund and thus determine the surplus or deficit in the fund 
as at 31 December 2015 under which the bank will compensate any shortfall that may arise from the investment 
fund.
The most important was the basic assumptions used by the actuary are as follows:  
- Death rates from the British Table A49-52 ULT.
- Disability rates from the experience of the Egyptian Social Security.
- Interest rate of 11% per annum for investments in Egyptian pounds, 5% per annum for U.S. dollar investments.
- Rates of wage increases ranging from 5% of the Egyptian pound, zero percent for the U.S. dollar.
- Unity method is used in the calculation of the estimated additional commitments and the present value of 
subscriptions (Unit Projected method).

We have audited the accompanying separate financial statements  of Arab African International  
Bank “Egyptian joint stock company” which comprise the balance sheet  as of “31 December 
2016”and the  statements of  income, changes in equity and cash flow statement for the year 
then ended and a summary of significant accounting policies and other explanatory notes.  
Management’s Responsibility for the separate financial statements 
These separate financial statements are the responsibility of bank management. Management 
is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these separate financial statements 
in accordance with the rules of preparation and presentation of the Bank’s separate 
financial statements issued by the Central Bank of Egypt on 16 December 2008 and with 
the requirements of applicable Egyptian laws and regulations.  This responsibility includes 
designing, implementing and maintaining internal control relevant to the preparation and 
fair presentation of separate financial statements that are free from material misstatement, 
whether due to fraud or error; selecting and applying appropriate accounting policies; and 
making accounting estimates that are reasonable in the circumstances.
Auditors’ Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these separate financial statements based 
on our audit.  We conducted our audit in accordance with Egyptian Standards on Auditing.

INTRODUCTION
A VISIONARY  
APPROACH
The last 15 years have been ones of exceptional growth for AAIB; 
growth that has catapulted us from a prominent Egyptian bank 
to a leading regional financial group. Throughout this journey, 
the Bank mastered the art of both qualitative and quantitative 
growth, which has seen us achieve numerous firsts, among which 
are being the first Egyptian bank with full-fledged presence 
in the GCC, the first bank to operate a standalone investment 
banking arm, and the first to embed sustainable practices 
throughout its operations. It is these firsts that have positioned 
AAIB as a visionary bank, not just in its core competency as a 
commercial bank, but as a steward of industry-wide change and 
a gateway for international business into the region. 
AAIB has for years led by example, having been the first bank 
to join the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC) and the first 
to adopt the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) well before they were formally introduced. In the past 12 
months we have gone a step further to align our strategy with 
the Egyptian government’s vision to boost financial inclusion 
as one of the key pillars of its economic reform agenda. The 
past year has also seen us successfully realize an important 
pillar of our growth story, one that has takes us from a financial

sustainable finance for the good of the economy, the financial

CHAIRMAN’S NOTE
CHAIRMAN’S 
NOTE
DEAR VALUED SHAREHOLDERS,
On behalf of the AAIB Board of Directors, it gives me great 
pleasure to present to you our 2017 Annual Report and financial 
statements for the year ending 31 December 2017. This year 
proffered both challenges and opportunities for AAIB as we took 
steps to adjust to the initial effects of the Egyptian government’s 
economic reform program while introducing new products, 
services, and business lines – including new channels to serve 
SME clients and microfinance arm Sandah.
Throughout 2017, businesses and the banking industry alike had 
to navigate a rapidly unfolding and new economic reality brought 
about by the rollout of the Egyptian government’s reform program. 
From the float of the pound and raising interest rates to the phase-
out of energy subsidies and fiscal consolidation measures – the 
government’s reform program was a bitter but necessary pill to 
swallow to reinvigorate an ailing economy and set us on a more 
sustainable and promising growth trajectory as a nation. 
Despite the unique economic challenges presented this 
year – including the flotation and subsequent devaluation of 
the Egyptian pound and interest rate hikes as high as 700 bps – 
AAIB achieved superior financial performance while acting as a 
crucial supporter and guide for our clients and investors. AAIB’s 
total net operating profit amounted to USD 357 million in 2017 
compared to USD 407 million recorded in 2016, which we see as

We also managed to grow our deposit base 24% y-o-y in 2017 
to USD 8.6 billion, an achievement that can be attributed to the 
attractiveness of our liability product and steady growth in our 
large number of branches. Overall, AAIB’s return on average 
equity recorded 16% in USD terms in 2017, inching down only 
slightly from 18% in the previous year. In context, the Bank has 
also been leading the industry with soundness in capital and 
highest productivity and efficiency ratios. 
Our financial success during the year was anchored by the 
numerous operational achievements. From bolstering our 
regional presence through our offshore branches, expanding 
our investment portfolio both in terms of geographic and sector 
reach, to enhancing our product and service offering throughout 
the diverse set of business lines under our umbrella, I am proud 
to say that we have not only maintained our status as  Egypt’s 
fastest growing bank, but remained a beacon of success in the 
industry while continuing to drive value for all stakeholders.

range of corporate clients by expanding into diverse sectors and

A NOTE FROM OUR VICE

DEAR VALUED SHAREHOLDERS,
“Visionary Banking” has become a mantra for bankers all around 
the world as they look to keep their businesses progressing 
successfully and navigate past the evolving challenges 
presented by an increasingly dynamic landscape. It is a call to 
see the big picture and understand the interconnections between 
the banking industry and the world around us. With the rise of 
new global trends – including sustainability and environmental 
concerns combined with the growing role of technology – the 
viability of the financial industry’s business model is being 
called into question. If we are to continue serving as anchors 
for the economy and ensure we avoid future financial crises, 
our measure of success needs to go beyond profit and return on 
equity and must include qualitative and quantifiable metrics for 
sustainable value creation for all stakeholders. 
At AAIB, our “Visionary Banking” approach is our distinctive 
value, making us the country’s leading financial powerhouse. 
Despite a year shaped by immense challenges, AAIB has seen 
impressive financial performance while staying true to its 
reputation of being an industry pioneer. On a standalone basis, 
net profit for the year came in 2% higher at USD 255.5 million 
in 2017. Normalizing for fluctuations in foreign exchange rate 
– by translating 2016 local currency results at the applicable

OF DISTINCTION
Arab African International Bank (AAIB) is a leading regional 
financial institution and Egypt’s first Arab multinational bank, 
having been incorporated in 1964 by Special Law as a joint 
venture between the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) and the 
Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA). Established as a corporate 
and investment bank, with a USD-based equity and authority to 
deal in USD and other foreign currencies, AAIB aimed to build 
a financial institution that would leverage its long-cultivated 
reputational standing, pioneering financial products, and 
geographic footprint to become the region’s financial backbone. 
The Bank’s incorporation was signed by the late Egyptian 
president Gamal Abdel Nasser and H.E. Gabr Al Ahmed Al Gabr 
Al Sabbah, Kuwait’s former crown prince, ensuring that it took its 
first steps with the strength and stamina of a solid establishment. 
Today, CBE and KIA, its founding shareholders, each hold 49.37% 
of the bank’s outstanding shares.
Since 2002, the Bank has pursued an aggressive growth 
strategy, not merely to become a lucrative institution but to create 
value for all stakeholders. By pioneering market expansion, the 
Bank has grown both organically and inorganically. Its acquisition 
of Misr America International Bank in 2005 and the loan and deposit 
portfolio of the sole representative office in Egypt of Canadian Nova

To maintain its positioning as the fastest-growing bank in

customer needs, AAIB sets out carefully measured, forward-
looking strategies each year with the underlying goal being to 
consistently create value for shareholders. AAIB’s strategic 
business objectives are backed by its Financial Planning & 
Performance Analysis department — the first to be established 
by an Egyptian bank — which works to facilitate the decision 
making while aligning the strategic objectives of individual lines

strategy centered on five distinct areas: Intensifying Investment 
and Corporate Finance, Tapping New Segments, Developing the 
Retail Business, Increasing Synergies with Financial Arms, and 
Moving Toward Digitalization. These planks are the foundation of 
the Bank’s three-year plan, which build on AAIB’s reputational 
stronghold in the Egyptian market, its regional prowess as the 
only private sector bank with presence in the Gulf region, and 
its thriving financial group.

MANAGEMENT 
DISCUSSION & 
ANALYSIS
AAIB delivers a strong set of results with key metrics 
improving across the board despite a challenging 
operational backdrop
2017 was by no means an ordinary year. The kick-off of the 
Egyptian government’s economic reform program ushered in a 
new set of market dynamics that affected businesses across. The 
float of the Egyptian pound in November 2016 saw the currency 
devalued by over 50%, presenting new challenges to an economy 
heavily dependent on imports from production inputs and raw 
materials to finished goods and services. Meanwhile, interest 
rate hikes of 700 bps since the float and during 2017 meant 
that businesses were faced with a significantly higher cost of 
debt, with opportunities for expansion and new investments 
being sidelined by a need to maintain a tight rein on expenses, 
maximize efficiency and protect profitability. 
Faced with a uniquely challenging operational backdrop, 
AAIB’s customers from retail individuals to corporate clients 
and strategic investors depended heavily on our institution to 
support them navigate these uncharted territories. Leveraging 
its reputation for service excellence and innovation, AAIB was 
able to deliver on its client demands and in turn continued 
its legacy of being the fastest growing bank in Egypt with an 
unmatched ability to create shareholder value.

POSITION

RETAIL BANKING
AAIB’s Retail division is one of the fastest growing in 
the nation, capitalizing on the Bank’s solid footing in the 
corporate and institutional banking segments
AAIB’s Retail Banking division offers a wide range of solutions 
tailored to the many personal financial needs of a large cross-
section of Egyptian populace: accounts and deposits, loans, 
credit and debit cards, wealth management, transaction 
banking, trade finance, payroll and merchant services, and 
more, making it one of the few banks in Egypt with a product 
portfolio of this breadth. Since its establishment, the Retail 
Banking division has grown from an ancillary service to AAIB’s 
largely corporate clients into a key growth driver for the Bank. By 
leveraging synergies within various divisions of the Bank, AAIB 
is, as of today, one of Egypt’s fastest growing retail banks, both 
in size and profitability, with a compound average growth rate of 
deposit and loan portfolios that has consistently outperformed 
market averages.
Setting itself apart from the competition, AAIB’s Retail 
Banking division used its deft touch in interacting with clients to 
discern their exact needs to provide tailored solutions. Thanks 
to the Bank’s long track record in catering to affluent clients and 
its strong reputation for service quality, AAIB’s Retail Banking 
division is able to personalize its solutions to suit its clients’ 
unique needs, helping it build a trusted relationship with them.

by which others in the industry are measured, with its dealing

record in the industry, seeing AAIB through fluctuating market 
conditions with resilience and unmatched expertise. It has grown 
to become the top licensed primary dealer bank in Egypt and one 
of the top five private banking treasury divisions in the country, 
providing some of the most innovative service solutions in the 
industry backed by the professionalism and carefully calculated 
expertise that epitomizes the AAIB brand today. 
AAIB’s award-winning TCM team offers expert, client-
centric services tailored to the needs of every customer in 
the areas of treasury, fixed income, capital markets, foreign 
exchange, derivatives, and cash and liquidity management. 
The division takes pride in the exceptional qualifications of its 
team members, all of which hold ACI Diplomas and a significant 
number being CFA charterholders. These qualifications coupled 
with an extensive in-house training structure allows TCM to

into the planning and execution of all the Bank’s operations,

and procedures that are strictly enforced to comply with the 
Bank’s overarching strategy to build and maintain a sustainable, 
transparent business model.

AAIB has a multiple defense-operating model where customer 
risk categorization is updated periodically. The Risk Management 
Group monitors and measures the risks to which the bank is 
exposed: credit risk, market risk, and operational risk, as well as 
concentration risk, banking book interest rate risk, funding risk, 
business risk, liquidity risk, and environmental and social risk.
As part of its ICAAP methodology, the Risk Management 
Group assesses the Bank’s base business plan and budget 
from a capital adequacy point. It provides forward-looking 
assessments and runs macroeconomic stress scenarios to 
reduce the Bank’s exposure to future macroeconomic stresses. 
The Risk Management Group prepares periodical reports to 
various management committees, as well as for the Board of 
Directors and its Risk Committee.

With the talent and hard work of some of the most driven IT 
professionals in the industry, the Information Security (IS) division 
designs, builds, and develops the layers of security that protect 
AAIB’s information assets. The division acts on all fronts that can 
impact the Bank’s information resources and the information of 
its customers and stakeholders, from security policies, IT asset 
inventory, and access controls to operations and communications 
security, incident management, and business continuity. 
To reduce risks to the lowest possible levels, the division follows 
a cyclic process that monitors, detects, prevents, protects, and 
measures impact on the Bank’s data.
Since 2016, the IS division has followed a strategy called 
“Defense-in-Depth” that implements layered security controls 
by addressing the following: 
• Information security policies and procedures
• IT operations management
• Physical security
• Network perimeter security
• Internal network security
• Applications security
• Hosts security (servers, desktops, and notebooks)
• Data security
These multiple layers of hardware and software controls ensure 
the confidentiality and integrity of the Bank’s information, as 
well as its availability for AAIB’s customers.

the IS team’s goal is to create a stronghold built from the most 
innovative and creative solutions for managing security threats

internal training programs and external offerings:
• All employees are provided equal access to L&D

• Employees are provided with all the training needed

career development, and the Bank offers opportunities 
to achieve these goals.

2017 IN REVIEW
Transparency and Information Sharing 
At AAIB, we believe educating clients about banking products 
and services is more important than promoting them. In saying 
that, transparency has been a key pillar for the division long 
before it was introduced as part of industry mandates. 
To enhance the knowledge and awareness of our clients, in 2011, 
we Introduced “Money Quotient Program (MQ)” the AAIB Financial 
Literacy series. The series aims at improving the customers’ 
understanding of banking and finance via a considerable campaign 
of bilingual (English/Arabic) videos on all social media platforms 
for educating existing and potential clients. It explains what a bank 
is and the difference between types of loans, credit cards, mutual 
funds, and bank accounts. As we consider financial advisory 
essential, the series shares advice on managing investments, 
retirement accounts, and money savings plans. A weekly featured 
financial tip helps viewers measure their money IQ. 
In-Branch Experience 
AAIB branches maintain standardized interior guidelines that pay 
tribute to its classical heritage while embracing automation and 
digital screens to perfect the customer experience. Because the 
in-branch experience is one of our most important customer touch 
points, the division was a major collaborator with AAIB Egypt’s retail 
team in branch expansion. As part of mapping AAIB Egypt’s network 
of new and relocated branches, remote and vital areas were

waste significantly harm the environment. The goal is to 
encourage behavioural change and influence new generations.

2017 IN REVIEW
AAIB has helped make El Gouna International Squash Tournament 
one of the seven top ranking international championships. Since 
its inception in 2010, AAIB has been backing the tournament 
consistently believing in the capacities of Egyptian squash players.  
Egypt produces some of the world’s best squash players, and as 
one of the sport’s most prominent tournaments, El Gouna Open 
brings this recognition to the world.
To AAIB, this is far beyond sports’ sponsorships or corporate 
branding. We empower the Egyptian young athletes to achieve 
what they aspire to. Equip them to level up to the international 
standards, recognize their devotion, and exerted efforts.
AAIB has extended its support to entrepreneurs in Egypt at an 
early point in time. In 2013, AAIB co-founded the AUC Venture 
Lab - the first academic-based incubator in Egypt. 
AUC Venture Lab supports early-stage start-ups chosen 
based on the project’s novelty, scalability, and commercialization 
potential, and the dedication of the team. AAIB pioneered the lab 
in the belief that empowering and facilitating Egypt’s inventive 
and committed entrepreneurs to reach their goals should be a 
core value for the country.
 AUC Venture Lab connects start-ups with AUC’s network to 
turn their innovative ideas into viable ventures that contribute to 
economic growth, competitiveness, and job creation.

KEY ELEMENTS OF AAIB’S 
GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK 
AAIB BOARD OF DIRECTORS
AAIB’s Board structure is consistent with best practice and 
CBE directives, which promote the separation between the 
roles of the Chairman as a non-executive and the Executive 
Director of the Bank.  The Bank’s Board of Directors consists 
of eight qualified members: seven non-executive directors 
(NEDs) including the Chairman of the Board and one Executive 
Director.  
The Board is responsible for the overall stewardship of the 
Bank, including the establishment of AAIB’s strategic direction, 
overseeing the achievement of its long-term goals, as well as 
overseeing the effectiveness of internal controls. The Board of 
Directors is also responsible for ensuring that business activities 
are aligned with the interests of AAIB’s main stakeholders, and 
within the framework of governing laws and regulations and the 
Bank’s approved policies.  In 2017, Mr. Osamah Al-Furaih’s term 
ended and he was succeeded by Mr. Adnan Al-Sager.  Over the 
course of FY2017, AAIB’s Board of Directors convened six times.
KEY 2017 GOVERNANCE ACHIEVEMENTS 
Over the course of FY2017, the Board undertook the following:
• Full review of standard reports to be submitted to the 
Board and its committees.
• Formal guidelines for the self-assessment of the Board 
and its committees.
• Recomposition of Board committees.
• Completed a self-assessment exercise of the Board and 
its committees.

Board Committees
The Board is assisted in the discharge of its responsibilities by 
five committees: Audit (BAC), Risk (BRC), Corporate Governance 
(CGC), Remuneration (RemCo), and the Executive Committee 
(ExCo).  All Board committees have formal well-defined terms of 
reference governing their activities, which are reviewed periodically 
to assess the adequacy of their respective charters and to ensure 
that they reflect regulatory requirements and best practices. With 
the exception of the BRC and the ExCo, board committees consist 
entirely of non-executive directors. Committees may engage external 
advisors to support their duties. Each committee, through its chair, 
reports to the Board with respect to its activities and with such 
recommendations as are deemed appropriate in the circumstances.

SUSTAINABLE  
FINANCE  
AAIB’s sustainable finance agenda encapsulates a holistic 
approach to finance to enable the Bank to create value for 
all stakeholders and steward industry change
Sustainable Finance is an integral part of the AAIB brand. 
The Bank’s journey with sustainable finance started when it 
seriously contemplated an aggressive growth strategy. At this 
point, AAIB recognized that growth has both a material and non-
material dimension. Its focus went beyond the single bottom 
line to pursuing the triple bottom line. The Bank thus made the 
connection between finance and the environment, society and 
governance since the early years of the millennium. 
Over half a century of industry expertise has given AAIB the 
acumen and insight to recognize the financial sector’s crucial 
role in value creation, not just for shareholders, but for the 
environment, the communities in which we live and work, and the 
business community at large. As the backbone of the Egyptian 
economy, banks - like AAIB- have a central obligation to instill, 
practice, and promote the tenets of sustainable finance. In 2003, 
AAIB became a forerunner in sustainable finance, setting up the 
foundations on which it has grown to become the cornerstone of 
industry change not just in Egypt, but the region. 
Having been one of the first banks to develop a corporate 
social responsibility (CSR) platform, our sustainability agenda

in sustainable finance across the region. Our purpose is 
embedding sustainable practices throughout our operations, to 
lead an industry-wide movement in sustainable finance through 
MOSTADAM — the first sustainable finance platform in the 
MENA region.
As the first bank in Egypt to become a signatory of the United 
Nations Global Compact (UNGC) in 2005 and upholding the essence 
of the Sustainability Development Goals (SDGs) well before they 
were even introduced, AAIB has set the standard in the local and 
regional market for sustainable development practices. Since 
then, our efforts have been backed by a distinguished network of 
global initiatives. In 2009, the Bank joined the EQUATOR PRINCIPLES 
(EP), a risk management framework adopted by financial 
institutions to determine, assess, and manage environmental

LONDON BENCHMARK GROUP (LBG), a UK-based organization

of corporate contribution to community development. In 2017, we

initiatives.

GLOBAL 
AFFILIATIONS
AAIB partners with several global affiliates to support its 
sustainability agenda and enhance its capacity to advocate for 
sustainable business practices in Egypt and the region 
As a pioneer of sustainable finance in the MENA region, AAIB had 
developed partnerships with leading global organizations focused 
on corporate social responsibility (CSR) and sustainability. 
Our affiliates have provided us with the resources and support 
needed to substantiate our many sustainability “firsts” in 
the Egyptian and regional banking sectors. We were the first 
Egyptian bank to establish a CSR agenda, publish a sustainability 
report, introduce social and environmental risk management 
and comply with Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) standards. With 
the establishment of MOSTADAM in 2014, we became the first 
regional bank to launch a sustainable finance platform. 
For more than a decade, our global partners have guided our 
adoption of the latest international standards for sustainable 
business operations. This in turn has allowed AAIB to serve as 
a role model for other Egyptian and regional companies and 
to advocate for a greater commitment to sustainability within 
the private sector as a whole. Currently, AAIB partners with 
four organizations in support of its sustainability agenda: the 
UN Global Compact (UNGC), the United Nations Environment 
Programme Finance Initiative (UNEP FI), the Equator Principles 
(EP), and the London Benchmarking Group (LBG).

UN GLOBAL COMPACT
Today the UN Global Compact is the world’s largest CSR 
initiative supported by 9,792 companies in 164 countries. The 
UNGC asks companies to integrate ten principles focused on 
human rights, labor, the environment, and anti-corruption into 
their values and core operations. UNGC companies are also 
called to advocate for reform and broader adoption of high 
standards in these areas within the private sector as a whole.
In 2015, the United Nations’ member countries adopted a new 
plan for achieving global equality, ending poverty, and protecting 
the planet entitled Vision 2030. A key feature of this plan is the 
17 UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that member 
states, civil society groups, and UNGC companies are called on 
to comply with and advance. This comprehensive set of principles 
encompasses issues such as poverty, gender equality, access to 
education, environmental sustainability, health and wellbeing, 
and more. Companies report their progress in upholding the 
UNGC’s principles and advancing the SDGs through annual 
Communications on Progress (COPs) submitted to the UNGC and 
sustainability reports – including those in compliance with the 
UN’s Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) standards – published for 
company shareholders and the wider public. 
Since becoming the first Egyptian bank to join the UNGC

EQUATOR PRINCIPLES
The EPs are a risk management framework designed to help 
global financial institutions identify, assess, and develop strategies 
to manage the environmental and social risks of various projects. 
Today, over 80 financial institutions based in more than 30 
countries and operating in over 100 countries have signed on to 
become Equator Principles Financial Institutions (EPFIs).

countries and operating in over 100 countries have signed on to 
become Equator Principles Financial Institutions (EPFIs).
The principles offer standards for conducting due diligence 
and making responsible decisions in relation to risk. Additionally, 
the EPs guide companies in raising the quality and robustness 
of their internal and environmental and social policies. These 
principles apply to four financial projects: project finance 
advisory services, project finance, project-related corporate 
loans, and bridge loans. Institutions that adopt the EPs agree 
not to provide project finance or related corporate loans to 
projects in which a client will not or cannot comply with the EPs.
When AAIB adopted the EPs in 2009, it became the first EPFI in 
Egypt and the second in the MENA region. To comply with these 
principles, AAIB conducts a social and environmental audit prior 
to authorizing corporate financing in excess of USD 10 million 
and bridge loans in excess of USD 2 million. The bank produced 
its first EP report in 2010 and continues to engage in annual 
reporting activities. In 2017, the EPs served as key guidelines in 
drafting and implementing customized environmental, social, 
and governance (ESG) standards in line with the International 
Financial Corporation’s Sustainability Framework.

WE OWE IT  
TO EGYPT FOUNDATION
AAIB’s We Owe it to Egypt Foundation goes beyond banking 
and into the frontier of social change, setting the trend for 
sustainable innovation in the fields of health and education
Established in January 2007, AAIB’s We Owe it to Egypt 
Foundation is a non-profit social development organization 
dedicated to improving every Egyptian’s quality of life through 
the enhancement of health and education services across 
the country. AAIB is the first bank in Egypt, and the region, 
to establish such an organization, beginning with the Bank’s 
pioneering and foundational initiatives in renovating public 
sector hospitals since 2003. 
Shortly following the turn of the century, AAIB looked up from 
its top-performing banking operations and outward, setting its 
sights on backing the communities in which it operated and 
making a sustainable, positive impact. Health and education 
were two pressing and obvious pillars for development in 
Egypt, prompting AAIB to lay the foundations of its sustainability 
agenda on these planks, which paved the way for what would 
then become the We Owe it to Egypt Foundation.
One of the biggest problems plaguing the healthcare sector 
in Egypt is high demand, with not nearly enough facilities to 
accommodate high levels of congestions and patients every 
day. As a result, waiting lists at public hospitals remain a major 
obstacle for any citizen wishing to receive proper care. In

patriotic call for action, one that issues a nationwide invitation 
for corporation and for individuals to seize the opportunity to 
address and end the issues currently plaguing Egypt. Firm in 
its belief that every Egyptian deserves to live the healthiest and 
most productive life possible, the Foundation strives to become 
a driver of significant impact and sustainable development of 
health and education in Egypt.
The Foundation’s primary mission is to enact a nationwide 
pooling of resources towards community development projects, 
directing its efforts toward improving the quality and reach of 
healthcare and education services.

AUTOMATION
Almost all public hospitals in Egypt keep their patient files 
exclusively on paper, risking patients’ lives as bureaucratic 
procedures grow longer and accidental loss remains a strong 
possibility. Setting the trend for other non-profit organizations, 
the Foundation signed a cooperation agreement with the 
Ministry of Administrative Development to initiate and fund the 
Ministry’s push to digitize and computerize the files of several 
public hospitals, enabling the automated archiving of patient 
data on computers, and linking them seamlessly to other 
hospital networks. 
With past successes including the automation of the Abu 
Al-Rish Al-Munira Hospital, the Foundation believes in the 
importance of digitally upgrading and outfitting medical

healthcare and education.

 AL MANIAL HOSPITAL
As part of the Foundation’s approach to ensure the 
achievement of the highest quality healthcare and education, 
it was necessary to automate hospitals to quickly save and 
retrieve patient data and record medical files, which could 
then be used for scientific research.
In 2017, the Foundation outfitted Al-Manial University 
Hospital (previously Kasr Al Aini Hospital) with computers and 
quickly documented patient data online at a total value of EGP 1 
million. The two phases of the project have been completed and 
will be inaugurated in May 2018.
ASSIUT UNIVERSITY 
The Foundation also took on another automation project during 
the year; the computerization of the Assiut University’s South 
Egypt Cancer Institute. The project successfully linked patients’ 
medical data to the National Cancer Registry at a cost of EGP 1.016 
million. The registry, which is currently being linked to the National 
Institute of Oncology, will allow for 12 tumor centers nationwide to 
create a comprehensive online database across Egypt. The project 
is scheduled to be completed by the end of October 2018.

SPECIALIZED MEDICAL 
CARAVANS
During 2017, the Foundation was particularly interested in 
sponsoring medical caravans to provide the best medical services 
to citizens living in remote areas and the poorest villages. 
Under this umbrella, the cooperation agreement between 
the Foundation and the Moroccan Foundation was renewed for 
the fourth year in a row. Five eye exam caravans were funded 
and dispatched to a number of villages in Beni Suef, Fayoum, 
and Qena at a total value of EGP 296,000. The caravans 
conducted more than 1,717 medical services, including the 
provision of 764 glasses and 293 free medications. They also 
transferred 300 cases to general hospitals for further tests, 
resulting in 236 cataract removals and lens implantations. 
AIN SHAMS UNIVERSITY
The Foundation also renewed its cooperation with the Faculty of 
Medicine, Ain Shams University, dispatching medical caravans 
for the second year in a row to a number of villages in Fayoum. 
The Foundation provided the medical convoys’ laboratories 
with equipment for blood tests, allowing them to conduct 2,818 
medical examinations and 1,302 blood tests, which uncovered 
63 cases of hepatitis C.  
THE FOUNDATION IN 2018
As the Foundation looks to the future, it aims to provide more 
health services outside of the Cairo governorate and spread to 
the Delta and Upper Egypt, providing healthcare to people living 
in underdeveloped and remote areas.

2-SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES 
The principal accounting policies applied in the preparation of these financial statements are set out 
below. These policies have been consistently applied to the Periods presented, unless otherwise stated.  
A-Basis of preparation
The separate financial statements of the bank have been prepared in accordance with the rules of 
preparation and presentation approved by the Central Bank of Egypt on 16 December 2008, under 
the historical cost convention modified to re-evaluate financial assets and financial liabilities held for 
trading, financial assets and financial liabilities classified at inception at fair value through profits or 
losses and financial investments available for sale, and all derivative contracts.
B-Subsidiaries and associates
B-1Subsidiaries
Subsidiaries are all entities (including special purpose entities) over which the bank has owned 
directly or indirectly the power to govern the financial and operating policies, generally accompanying 
a shareholding of  more than one half of the voting rights. The existence and effect of potential voting 
rights that are currently exercisable or convertible are considered when assessing whether the bank 
controls another entity.
B-2 Associates
Associates are all entities over which the bank has direct or indirect significant influence but not 
control, generally accompanying a shareholding of between 20% and 50% of the voting rights.

E-2 Loans and receivables
Loans and receivables are non-derivative financial assets with fixed or determinable payments that 
are not quoted in an active market, other than:
• Those that The bank intends to sell immediately or in the short term, which are classified as 
held for trading, and those that The bank upon initial recognition designates as at fair value 
through profit or loss;
• Those that The bank  upon initial recognition designates as  available for sale; or 
• Those for which the bank may not recover substantially all of its initial investment, other 
than because of credit deterioration.  
E-3 Held-to-maturity financial assets
Held-to-maturity investments are non-derivative financial assets with fixed or determinable 
payments and fixed maturities that the bank’s management has the intention and ability to hold to 
maturity. If the bank was to sell other than an insignificant amount except for specific situations, the 
entire category would be reclassified as available for sale. 
E-4 Available-for-sale financial assets 
Available-for-sale investments are non-derivative financial assets intended to be held for an indefinite 
Period of time, which may be sold in response to needs for liquidity or changes in interest rates, 
exchange rates or equity prices.

FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
The criteria that the bank uses to determine that there is objective evidence of an impairment loss 
include:
• Significant financial difficulties of the issuer or obligor;
• Breach of contract such as default in interest or principal payment;
• It becomes probable that the borrower will enter bankruptcy or other financial reorganization;
• Deterioration of the borrower’s competitive position.
• The bank, for economic or legal reasons relating to the borrower’s financial difficulties, 
granting to the borrower a concession that the bank would not otherwise consider.
• Deterioration in the value of collateral.
• Downgrading the credit status.  
The existence of clear data that indicates measurable decrease in estimated future cash flows 
from a group of financial assets are  considered as objective evidence of impairment for that group.  
Irrespective of the ability of identifying that reduction for each individual asset.e.g, the increase in 
number of repayment defaults for a particular banking product. 
The estimated Period between a losses occurring and its identification is determined by local 
management for each identified portfolio. In general, the Period used vary between three months 
and twelve months.
The bank first assesses whether objective evidence of impairment exists individually for financial 
assets that are individually significant, and individually or collectively for financial assets that are not

The bank’s activities expose it to a variety of financial risks and those activities involve the analysis, 
evaluation, acceptance and management of some degree of risk or combination of risks. Taking risk 
is core to the financial business, and the operational risks are an inevitable consequence of being in 
business. The bank’s aim is therefore to achieve an appropriate balance between risk and return and 
minimize potential adverse effects on the bank’s financial performance.
The most important types of risk are credit risk, liquidity risk, market risk and other operational 
risk. Market risk includes currency risk, interest rate and other price risk.

Debt securities and treasury bills
For debt securities and treasury bills external rating such as (Standard & Poor’s) rating or their 
equivalents are used by the bank for managing of the credit risk exposures. In case such ratings are 
unavailable, internal rating methods are used that are similar to those used for credit customers. The 
investment in those securities and bills are viewed as a way to gain a better credit quality mapping 
and maintain a readily available source to meet the funding requirements at the same time.

lending limits when appropriate.
